#5525. A little-known protein could be a powerful weapon against Alzheimer’s

A protein that helps protect the brain may offer scientists a promising new way to fight Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Researchers have discovered that increasing levels of this protein can reduce the buildup of toxic tangles associated with brain damage, while also helping preserve the connections that allow nerve cells to communicate.

The findings, published in Science Advances by scientists at Sanford Burnham Prebys, suggest that strengthening the brain's own protective mechanisms could eventually lead to new treatments for neurodegenerative diseases. In experiments with mice, the researchers found that boosting the protein reduced several damaging changes associated with Alzheimer's, including brain shrinkage and the accumulation of abnormal tau proteins.

The discovery is particularly significant because tau plays an essential role in keeping healthy brain cells functioning. Under normal conditions, tau proteins help stabilize microtubules, tiny structures that provide internal support to neurons and help maintain the intricate networks of the nervous system.

In Alzheimer's and several related disorders, however, tau proteins can become abnormal and stick together, forming harmful clumps known as tau tangles. These tangles disrupt the normal functioning of nerve cells and are associated with cognitive decline and neuronal death. Diseases characterized by abnormal tau accumulation are collectively called tauopathies.

A Protective Protein With a Surprising Role in Alzheimer's

The researchers investigated a protein called sorting-related receptor with A-type repeats (SORLA), which has already attracted scientific attention for its potential role in protecting the brain against Alzheimer's disease.

Previous studies have shown that SORLA can help limit the production and accumulation of amyloid-beta, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's. Amyloid-beta can build up into plaques in the brain, making it one of the disease's major pathological hallmarks alongside tau tangles.

"In the last 15 or 20 years, considerable data has come out from our lab and other groups showing that SORLA can suppress one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer's disease -- amyloid-beta generation and accumulation," said Timothy Huang, PhD, assistant professor in the Center for Neurologic Diseases at Sanford Burnham Prebys.

"Very little was known, however, about whether SORLA affected the tau tangles reflected on the other side of the coin in Alzheimer's disease."

To investigate this question, the scientists developed a mouse model by breeding animals engineered to produce additional human SORLA with mice that develop tau tangles, brain atrophy, and cognitive impairments. This allowed them to examine whether higher SORLA levels could reduce tau accumulation and protect against the damage it causes.

Boosting SORLA Reduces Toxic Tau and Brain Shrinkage

The results revealed that additional SORLA provided protection against several processes that contribute to tau tangles and the progression of neurodegenerative disease.

One important effect involved a process called hyperphosphorylation. This occurs when too many phosphate groups attach to tau proteins, altering their behavior and contributing to the development of harmful tangles. Higher SORLA levels reduced this abnormal modification.

The protein also limited the ability of misfolded tau to act as "seeds" that encourage other tau proteins to clump together. This seeding process can help toxic tau aggregates multiply and spread their damaging effects.

Beyond reducing tau abnormalities, SORLA helped preserve synapses, the specialized connections through which neurons communicate. It also protected synaptic plasticity, the brain's ability to strengthen or modify those connections, which is essential for learning, memory, and normal cognitive function.

"When you upregulate SORLA, you can suppress the negative effects found in tauopathies," said Huijie Huang, PhD, a staff scientist in the Huang lab at Sanford Burnham Prebys and lead author of the study.

"We found there was less brain atrophy and less tau accumulation, which was very exciting to see."

Removing the Protein Makes Brain Damage Worse

After observing the benefits of increasing SORLA, the researchers examined what would happen if the protein were missing entirely.

SORLA is produced using instructions encoded by a gene called Sorl1. Some people carry mutations that interfere with this gene's function, potentially disrupting the production or activity of the protective protein.

To investigate the consequences, the team studied genetically modified mice that lacked Sorl1 and therefore could not produce SORLA.

The results contrasted sharply with those seen in mice carrying additional copies of the protein. Instead of protecting against tau-related damage, the absence of SORLA made the harmful effects more severe.

"The opposite turned out to be true when we deleted the ability to produce SORLA proteins," said Tim Huang, senior and corresponding author of the manuscript. "A lack of SORLA exacerbated the harmful effects observed in tauopathies."

These contrasting results provided further evidence that SORLA plays an important protective role in the brain and may influence how severely tau-related diseases progress.

A New Clue Could Lead to Alzheimer's Treatments

To understand why changing SORLA levels had such different effects, the researchers examined the molecular activity of individual brain cells and the surrounding tissue.

They combined advanced sequencing methods to measure protein levels and gene activity in individual cells with techniques that map where RNA and proteins are located within brain tissue. This detailed approach helped reveal how SORLA influences the biological processes involved in neurodegeneration.

The analysis showed that increasing SORLA helped prevent harmful changes in protein production at synapses while also suppressing other mechanisms associated with tauopathy progression.

The researchers also discovered that higher SORLA levels reduced abnormal gene activity in glial cells. These cells perform several essential functions in the nervous system, including supporting, maintaining, and protecting neurons. Changes in glial cell activity can contribute to the progression of neurodegenerative diseases.

One finding was especially intriguing because it pointed toward a potential target for existing medications.

"One particularly notable finding that we can build on is the upregulation of a member of the plexin-B family of receptors in the absence of SORLA," said Huijie Huang.

Plexin-B receptors are proteins involved in cellular signaling, helping cells respond to information from their surroundings. The increased activity of a receptor in this family when SORLA was absent suggests that this signaling pathway could be involved in some of the damaging changes associated with tau disorders.

Importantly, drugs capable of targeting this family of receptors already exist, raising the possibility that scientists could investigate whether they might be useful against tau-related dementia.

"There are unique drugs that can target this class of receptors that we may be able to apply to tau-related dementia disorders," said Tim Huang. "One potential future direction is to repurpose these drugs to target overactivation of glial cells and perhaps reverse some of the phenotypes in tauopathies."

The Next Step Toward Human Alzheimer's Research

Although the findings are encouraging, the protective effects were demonstrated in mice, and more research is needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans.

The team now hopes to investigate how individual types of brain cells respond when SORLA levels increase or decrease. One planned approach involves transplanting human neurons or glial cells into mouse brains, allowing researchers to examine the effects of different SORLA mutations in a living brain affected by disease.

"Mouse cells and human cells are different," said Tim Huang. "Because we're looking at human disease, it's more informative if we can observe the modulation and dysfunction of SORLA in the context of a human cell inside of a diseased brain environment."

These experiments could help clarify how SORLA protects neurons from toxic tau accumulation and why disruptions in its function make neurodegeneration worse.

Ultimately, the researchers hope that a deeper understanding of this protective protein will reveal new treatment strategies, either by enhancing SORLA's activity or by repurposing existing drugs to interfere with damaging cellular pathways. Such approaches could eventually offer new ways to combat Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia driven by toxic tau tangles.

The study was supported by the National Institutes of Health, National Cancer Institute and National Institute on Aging.

#5524. The European Competitiveness Fund, the Backbone of a Modern European Investment Policy

European businesses call for a robust, well-funded European Competitiveness Fund

Dear Chancellors, Prime Ministers, Presidents,

Europe is losing ground in technological leadership and struggles to scale strategic technologies, while volatile energy costs and external dependencies continue to dampen business confidence.

Europe’s path to enduring technological leadership relies on our ability to scale strategic technologies. By stabilising energy costs, providing a path to clean industrial renewal and cultivating European resilience, we are laying the groundwork for robust business and investors’ confidence. Public investment has a crucial role to play to address these vital challenges. We require a smarter, more strategic investment policy for Europe.

We, more than 75 undersigned businesses, call on European leaders to agree to a Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) commensurate with Europe’s challenges, to protect its investment capacity and place long-term productivity growth, resilience and decarbonisation at its core. We believe the European Competitiveness Fund (ECF) represents a step-change in the EU’s investment policy and must be strengthened in the remaining negotiations.

The ECF with its toolbox projects the ambition to provide tailored support to the investment and scale-up challenge Europe faces. This is a positive evolution of the EU funding landscape. With a bigger role for the EU’s derisking instrument InvestEU, the ECF can become Europe’s modern investment vehicle with an increased use of guarantees, loans and equity to unlock strategic investments.

At the same time, non-repayable support needs to be dedicated to scaling up sectors that deliver high strategic value but cannot yet secure commercial capital in Europe. Ramp-up support for Europe’s cleantech manufacturing, including support for OpEx, is needed to make Europe’s bid to regain technological leadership credible.

The advisory services for SMEs and the single access portal promises a simpler access to funding for firms across Europe. If successful, the ECF can pool additional national funds through merit-based procedures open to eligible projects across the single market to bring further alignment and synergies into European industrial development.

Europe’s energy import dependency has become a strategic vulnerability for European businesses. To increase our economic resilience, the EU must prioritise investments into energy sovereignty. Incentives need to pivot capital allocation away from fossil fuel infrastructure, and towards clean energy and electrification. From 2028, the next MFF should not support new fossil-fuel infrastructure that prolongs dependency on fossil fuels, while providing narrowly defined safeguards for security of supply. We need steering mechanisms to reduce fossil fuel dependencies. EU funding can help to tackle high upfront costs and derisk the switch to cleaner and more reliable energy. Otherwise, long investment cycles create severe fossil fuel lock-in effects that threaten our operational autonomy with increasingly volatile fossil energy prices.

Europe’s investment gap cannot be solved by a smarter, more strategic funding approach alone. The confidence into European competitiveness needs to translate into a sizable budget for the clean transition to have lasting impact. The Commission proposes an average annual budget of €3.3 billion for a clean transition and industrial decarbonisation window of the ECF. This number is dwarfed by recurring estimates of the annual climate investment deficit of €344 billion. At the same time, according to the OECD, industrial subsidies have reached the highest levels since the financial crisis 2008.

We urge European leaders to respond to the evolving investment environment and adopt the European Parliament’s proposal to increase the size of the ECF by €26.6 billion and to allocate a substantial share of the additional funding for industrial decarbonisation and clean transition. The more efficient use of financial instruments and a strategic prioritisation can improve the impact of EU funding but cannot substitute the investment needs Europe is facing to boost competitiveness and security.

The next long-term budget and the European Competitiveness Fund must become the investment trigger for European businesses to regain competitiveness at the global scale, based on clear incentives and regulatory certainty. We businesses urge leaders to demonstrate a long-term vision and make the ECF the cornerstone of a new EU green industrial strategy.

#5523. Solar Industry Supports BAAJA While Environmental Orgs Oppose It

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) is an interesting piece of legislation. It is getting a ton of support from the solar sector, but it is heavily opposed by environmental organizations.

Following the passage of BAAJA in the US Senate the other day, Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), stated the following: “America is now one step closer to lower energy costs, more clean energy and a more reliable electric grid. Senators Lee, Capito, Heinrich, and Whitehouse deserve tremendous credit for advancing this bipartisan bill.”

The organization adds some more detail and why it thinks this is such a good piece of legislation: “SEIA analysis shows that BAAJA could unlock 167 gigawatts of additional solar capacity between 2028 and 2035, bringing solar to over 18% of U.S. electricity generation by 2035. The analysis finds that the bill’s reforms could reduce cumulative power sector CO2 emissions by approximately 20% and avoid $54 billion in public health damages.”

That sounds very appealing, doesn’t it? Why wouldn’t we want that?

Well, the Sierra Club argues the bill goes in quite the opposite direction. The storied organization states the following: “While a rogue president is waging a war on clean energy, the Senate rushed a deeply flawed bill that furthers the buildout of fossil fuels, strips away power from communities and Tribes, threatens our clean water and public lands, and endangers wildlife. The House of Representatives has an equal voice in the legislative process. They must reject the Senate’s fast-tracked bill and demand debate and consideration to deliver for the people, not corporate polluters and Donald Trump. The American people made a clear call merely weeks ago: our elected leaders must address soaring costs and a corrupt system that prioritizes corporate polluter profits over our health, our wallets, and our future.”

It seems the issue is that BAAJA would make it much easier to put up power plants, skipping all kinds of environmental protections. That is why Republicans support it in the first place — they are always keen to plow through environmental protections. The reason SEIA supports it is clear enough — the organization is just thinking about solar power plants and looking at the potential for more growth in the industry, especially considering the fact that solar is now typically the cheapest option for new power capacity and has been dominating new installations.

So, the question is: would BAAJA really disproportionately support solar power, or would it lead to a lot more fossil fuel power plants and an edge to the old, dirty power technologies? Can the legislation be both good and bad, or is someone getting this wrong?

#5522. Less Intensive Follow-Up of Lung Nodules May Result in Larger Cancers

— Study suggests a return to more intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules

A less intensive approach to monitoring newly detected small lung nodules failed to meet noninferiority criteria compared with a more intensive strategy, and may result in larger cancers at diagnosis, a cluster randomized pragmatic trial showed.

Among the patients with lung cancer, 36.3% of those in the less intensive group had cancers larger than 20 mm at diagnosis compared with 27.7% in the more intensive group, reported Michael K. Gould, MD, of the Kaiser Permanente Bernard J. Tyson School of Medicine in Pasadena, California, and colleagues.

After adjustment, size progression to larger than 20 mm was 7 percentage points (95% CI -2.0 to 15.9) more common in the less intensive group than the more intensive group, which exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of 5 percentage points, but was not statistically significant.

"Although neither group was clearly superior in the main analysis, we cautiously advise guideline developers to consider returning to the prior, more intensive recommendations for follow-up of small nodules, particularly in younger persons," the authors wrote in the Annals of Internal Medicine.

Indeed, a subgroup analysis showed that tumor progression was significantly more likely among younger patients in the less intensive group.

"We weren't able to validate the less intensive approach reflected in the current guidelines -- we weren't able to demonstrate noninferiority," Gould told MedPage Today.

In addition, "progression in size and stage are more common than one would think, perhaps suggesting that the whole idea of a CT follow-up strategy be reconsidered," he said. "When we see one-third of patients having progression, we need to do better."

Given the frequency of size progression in both groups, "newer approaches to follow-up for patients with small pulmonary nodules, including volumetric measurement, novel biomarkers, and radiomic tools, should be rigorously evaluated," Gould and team wrote.

The "Watch the Spot" trial enrolled 34,686 participants at 14 healthcare systems between March 2017 and July 2019. Mean age was 64.5, and 50.8% were women. All had a newly identified pulmonary nodule measuring 15 mm or less in diameter on a diagnostic or screening chest CT scan, defined as the index scan.

The protocols for less and more intensive CT follow-up were modeled on current and prior recommendations from the Fleischner Society and the Lung CT Screening Reporting and Data System (Lung-RADS).

Lung cancer was diagnosed within 27 months of nodule identification in 1.5% of those in the less intensive group and 1.4% of those in the more intensive group.

The median nodule size on the index CT scan was 9 mm, and 70% of all cancers were detected incidentally. More than 25% of lung cancers were diagnosed in participants with nodules measuring 6 mm or less in diameter at the time of detection on the index CT scan.

Median tumor size at diagnosis was 16 mm in the less intensive group compared with 15 mm in the more intensive group, and stage III or IV cancer was somewhat more common in the less intensive group (31.4%) than in the more intensive group (28.6%).

Adherence to protocol-based follow-up was "poor" in both study groups, the authors observed -- 42% in the less intensive group and 45% in the more intensive group. After adjustment among these patients, diagnosis with progression to a tumor size larger than 20 mm was more common in the less intensive group by 14.9 percentage points.

"Adherence is important," Gould observed. "While we're waiting for newer approaches -- whether it's volumetric measurement or novel biomarkers -- the poor adherence we observed in our study represents a very important opportunity for quality improvement."

#5521. The LiTime Lares K1 Expandable Plug & Play Kitchen Backup — CleanTechnica Tested

I spent 35 years in the Tampa suburbs, so I pay attention to backup power when a storm  is coming. Last year I tested the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 portable power station for CleanTechnica. That unit is meant to be carried around. The LiTime Lares K1 is different: a plug-in kitchen backup battery you leave in place and hook up to a refrigerator and also use to power your small kitchen appliances. First I’ll go through the specs and how it compares with a portable station like the Elite 100 V2, then I’ll give my test results.

LiTime launched the Lares K1 in the US on October 20, 2026. It is a split system: a slim inverter charger paired with a separate 2,304 watt-hour LiFePO4 battery (51.2 volts, 45 amp-hours). You can add up to four batteries, which brings the total to 9,216 watt-hours. The battery is rated for 4,000 cycles, and LiTime backs it with a 5-year warranty.

The inverter puts out 2,000 watts continuously and 4,000 watts of surge power for one second, as a pure sine wave at 120 volts. Adding batteries does not raise that output. You just get more runtime. There are two AC outlets, one on each side of the inverter. I did not see any USB ports listed.

You can charge it at up to 1,500 watts from a wall outlet and up to 800 watts from solar (12 to 60 volts). Combined input is capped at 1,500 watts. LiTime does not put a charge time on the main product page. If you divide 2,304 watt-hours by the 1,500-watt wall input, you get about 90 minutes from empty to full. That is a rough estimate. Charging usually slows down as you get close to 100%, the same way an EV does, and their FAQ later puts the theoretical time at about 1.7 hours if you figure 90% charging efficiency.

The inverter charger weighs about 10.1 pounds. LiTime does not list the battery weight, but I weighted it after I took it out of the packaging and it was about 52 pounds. With the floor stand, the two modules stood up together are 20.47 inches wide, 30.71 inches tall, and 3.94 inches deep. It runs at about 40 decibels (which is very quiet) and switches over to battery in 10 milliseconds or less. It has a touchscreen, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth 5.0, and the LiTime app, plus a time-of-use mode so you can charge off-peak.

The price on LiTime’s site is $1,099.99, shown as $100 off. US preorders opened October 20, 2026, and when I checked, estimated delivery was November 24 to 27.

LiTime calls this “space-based” home backup. Instead of trying to power the whole house, you protect one room, in this case the kitchen. You plug the system into a wall outlet and plug the fridge into the K1. No electrician and no panel work. LiTime estimates about 24 hours of backup on a large side-by-side refrigerator (while I got a bit more than that in my testing) that uses about 2 kilowatt-hours a day, or about 99 hours with four batteries if the fridge is the only load. Depending on the load, it can also run a microwave, an air fryer, a toaster, or a coffee maker for a basic meal. Just don’t try to run them all at once. You can run two smaller loads at once, but a large load like a microwave or air fryer needs to be run by itself (you can keep your refrigerator plugged in too). LiTime says to allow for compressor startup if you also want to run one of those at the same time.

You can wall-mount it, stand it on the floor, or lean it against a wall, with the two modules together or apart. It comes with mounting hardware and two connection cables, 0.25 meters and 1.5 meters (about 10 inches and 5 feet). The battery housing is steel, and LiTime says the metal finish is meant to suit a kitchen. The inverter is rated IP20, so it stays indoors. LiTime says separating the inverter from the battery cuts down on heat transfer, which they claim helps the battery last longer. I have not measured that.

For a plug & play system, this is a new product category. There have been portable generators available for years that could be used for camping or appliance backup, but having a product tailored to a specific room is a new concept. The comparison they offer is this one-room approach versus a whole-house battery system, the kind that usually needs panel work and that will cost you about 10 times as much.

You can use this for camping or travel, but it isn’t built for it. With split modules, wall-mount hardware, only two AC outlets, and no USB ports, this is built for a permanent kitchen install, not something you toss in the car for a weekend trip.

I used my old Kill-A-Watt meter to have an independent measure of the draw on the battery from the refrigerator. During the test, I opened the refrigerator less than I normally would, but still opened it about 10 times.

Next I wanted to test it with my small kitchen appliances. First, one at a time; then, several at once. It is rated at 2000 watts continuous, but it should be able to surge up to 4000 watts for 1 second.

Notice that it pulls 2510 watts from the battery, but the load is only 2290 watts. Where did the other 220 watts go? That must be used by the inverter to convert DC to AC.

After 35 years of Tampa storm seasons, I’ve learned that the fridge is usually the first thing you worry about when the power goes out. The LiTime Lares K1 is built for exactly that. In my testing it kept our large side-by-side GE refrigerator running for almost 26 hours on one battery, a bit longer than LiTime’s own estimate of 24 hours. It then shut off cleanly to protect the appliance. Recharging from the wall took about 3 hours, with 80% back in about 2 hours.

It also handled my small kitchen appliances well. The air fryer, coffee maker, and refrigerator ran together at about 2,200 watts, a little over the rated 2,000. When I added the toaster to push it past its limits, it briefly put out about 3,140 watts and then dropped back to about 2,130 watts without shutting down. The app also showed about 220 watts lost in converting battery power to AC, which is worth keeping in mind when you estimate runtime.

It does have limits. There are only two outlets, no USB ports, and the battery weighs about 52 pounds, so this is a permanent kitchen install, not a camping generator. Adding batteries gives you more runtime, but not more output.

At $1,099.99, with no electrician or panel work needed and a 5-year battery warranty, the Lares K1 is an affordable way to protect your food and still cook a basic meal during an outage. It costs about a tenth of what a whole-house battery would. If kitchen backup is what you care about most, it’s well worth a look.

#5520. Sharper at Age 60: Later-Born Generations Have Slower Memory Decline

— Newer generations also entered old age with better memory scores

Recent generations entered old age with better memory, and their memory declined more slowly than that of earlier generations, longitudinal data from over 219,000 people showed.

Being born 10 years later was associated with a 10% higher memory score at age 60 (d=0.32 per decade), reported Anders Fjell, PhD, of the University of Oslo in Norway, and colleagues.

At every age, later-born cohorts showed a higher probability of having stable memory. Each decade of later birth was associated with 64% higher odds of being in a stable memory period (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.59-1.68, P<0.001), and 38% lower odds of meeting steep-decline criteria at the same age (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.55-0.70, P<0.001).

"The combined advantage is large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per decade decline in dementia incidence," Fjell and colleagues wrote in Nature Medicine.

"It's known that later-born generations score better on cognitive tests. What this study shows is that the memory changes we observe during aging have also slowed," Fjell told MedPage Today.

"By age 80, about half of the generational advantage comes from each of these sources," he added. "The second half is new, and the total advantage is large enough to account for the reported fall in dementia incidence at a given age in Western countries."

In 2020, an analysis of seven population-based cohort studies in the U.S. and Europe from the Alzheimer Cohorts Consortium showed that the incidence rate of dementia declined by 13% per decade consistently in studies from 1998 to 2015.

In the U.S., the number of people living with dementia is projected to rise sharply as populations age, but dementia incidence among Medicare beneficiaries is falling.

To better understand recent trends, Fjell and colleagues evaluated over 783,000 memory assessments from more than 219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies in the U.S. and Europe who were followed for up to 30 years. Cohorts came from the U.S. Health and Retirement Study; the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing; the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe; the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing; and the Longitudinal Aging Study Amsterdam. Participants were ages 50 and older at baseline.

The researchers focused on verbal episodic memory as assessed by word-list recall, an indicator of Alzheimer's-related cognitive decline. Substudies assessed hippocampal volume change.

The slower decline of later-born generations was mirrored by slower hippocampal atrophy, the researchers observed. The fastest decliners had the most improvements over time.

The Lancet Commission estimated that nearly half of global dementia cases may be prevented or delayed through lifestyle and environmental changes, Fjell and co-authors pointed out. Because cognitive performance in adulthood correlates with childhood function, generational differences in memory decline may reflect early-life conditions that build cognitive capacity, they said.

Midlife factors like hypertension treatment and physical activity also may play a role, Fjell noted. "We cannot pinpoint the causes with certainty, since these are observational data," he said. "Likely drivers are the past century's improvements in education, childhood conditions, and cardiovascular health, which also means the findings support prevention as a life-course project rather than something that begins at 65."

There's no guarantee this positive development will continue, he pointed out. "The gains we see have been created by improvements in living conditions, education, and health throughout the 20th century, and they did not happen by themselves."

The study had several limitations, the researchers acknowledged. Faster decliners were less likely to complete all assessments over time, they said. Findings were from studies in high-income countries in Europe and North America, and may not apply to other parts of the world.

#5519. Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds

Vitamin C may do more than support everyday health. New research from the University of Waterloo suggests that it could also help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming during digestion. Using mathematical modeling, scientists investigated how vitamin C influences chemical reactions in the digestive system that have been linked to cancer risk.

Exposure to nitrates and nitrites has increased in North American diets over the past several decades. These compounds are found in cured meats such as bacon and salami, as well as in fruits and vegetables grown in soil or water affected by pollution. Although nitrates and nitrites contribute to important functions in the brain and cardiovascular system, they can also participate in potentially harmful reactions once they reach the stomach.

One of these reactions, called nitrosation, can produce substances that researchers suspect may contribute to cancer development. Understanding what causes these chemicals to form, and what might prevent their formation, has been a longstanding challenge.

Why Vitamin C Could Change the Cancer Risk Equation

"Since at least the 90s, researchers have been studying the link between cancer and these compounds, with conflicting results," said Dr. Gordon McNicol, a post-doctoral researcher in applied mathematics and the first author of the study. "Our work suggests that the presence of dietary Vitamin C may help explain these inconsistencies."

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed a mathematical model that simulates how nitrates and nitrites travel through the body and undergo chemical changes. The model incorporated several interconnected systems, including the salivary glands, stomach, small intestine, and plasma, the liquid portion of blood.

Their simulations revealed that vitamin C consumed alongside nitrates and nitrites may interfere with the formation of potentially harmful compounds. This could help explain why foods containing nitrates do not necessarily carry the same risks.

For example, leafy vegetables such as spinach naturally contain both nitrates and vitamin C. According to the model, the presence of vitamin C could limit the chemical reactions associated with cancer risk, potentially helping explain the protective effects suggested by some dietary research.

The researchers also explored whether vitamin C supplements might offer similar benefits when taken after eating.

Their findings suggest that taking vitamin C after each meal could moderately reduce the formation of nitrosation products associated with cancer risk. This effect could be particularly relevant when consuming foods containing nitrates and nitrites, including processed meats such as bacon and salami.

However, the results come from mathematical simulations rather than clinical trials. Although the model predicts that vitamin C can reduce the production of potentially harmful chemicals, further research is needed to determine whether this translates into a measurable reduction in cancer risk in humans.

New Clues for Future Cancer Prevention Research

The researchers believe their model could help scientists better understand the complicated relationship between diet, digestive chemistry, and cancer risk. It may also provide guidance for future experiments examining how nutritional choices influence the formation of potentially harmful compounds.

"This work provides a mechanistic roadmap for future clinical and laboratory studies by identifying the key interacting drivers of these potentially harmful chemical reactions, including nitrite exposure, antioxidant intake, meal timing, gastric conditions and oral microbiome activity," said Dr. Anita Layton, professor of applied mathematics and Canada 150 researcher chair. "This model can help researchers design more targeted experiments and interventions, focusing on when and in whom nitrosation is most likely to occur."

By identifying how factors such as vitamin C intake, meal timing, stomach conditions, and bacteria in the mouth interact, the model could help researchers develop more precise strategies for studying and potentially reducing cancer-related chemical reactions during digestion.

The study, "Vitamin C as a nitrosation inhibitor: A modelling study across dietary patterns and water quality," was published in the Journal of Theoretical Biology.

#5516. 13 Drugs Get Double-Digit Price Cuts in Medicare

— Savings of up to 84% will take effect in 2028

Medicare beneficiaries can look forward to saving up to 84% on drugs used to treat cancer, arthritis, and diabetes, among other conditions, thanks to the latest round of Medicare drug price negotiations.

"Every year, millions of seniors leave the pharmacy empty-handed because they can't afford their medication," CMS administrator Mehmet Oz, MD, MBA, said Monday in a press release. "The Trump administration is committed to use every tool at our disposal to negotiate fairer, more affordable prices to ease the burden on Medicare beneficiaries and help them get the care they need."

The negotiated prices will result in an estimated net savings for the Medicare program of 45%, or $9.2 billion, on 13 Medicare Part B and D drugs used to treat serious chronic conditions. CMS noted that when the negotiated prices go into effect in 2028, people enrolled in Medicare prescription drug coverage (i.e., Medicare Part D) would save under the defined standard benefit design an estimated $69 million in out-of-pocket costs. People with Medicare Part B coverage would save an estimated $395 million in out-of-pocket costs.

This is the third round of the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Program, which was established in 2022 under the Biden administration and allows the federal government to negotiate directly with manufacturers to lower prices for some of Medicare's most popular and expensive drugs.

The first round of negotiated prices went into effect in January 2026, covering drugs used by 8.8 million people on Medicare, with list price reductions ranging from 38% to 79%. The second round of negotiated prices will begin in January 2027, covering drugs used by 5.3 million people on Medicare, with list price reductions ranging from 38% to 85%.

This third round covers drugs used by 1.5 million people on Medicare, with list price reductions ranging from 34% to 84%, according to a CMS fact sheet. The listed drugs accounted for $25.6 billion in Medicare drug costs in 2025.

The drugs included in this round of price negotiations were:

Although tofacitinib (Xeljanz, Xeljanz XR) and omalizumab (Xolair) were originally selected for negotiation this cycle, they were not included in final negotiations because "before the end of or during the negotiation period" those drugs had generics or biosimilars approved for them, the agency said. Such drugs are not eligible for negotiation under the Medicare price negotiation program.

Healthcare groups were generally happy with the negotiation outcome. "Voters made clear in this month's midterm elections that families are fed up with the high cost of healthcare, and prescription drug prices are a big part of the problem," Anthony Wright, CEO of Families USA, said in a statement. "Medicare negotiation is showing itself to be a successful solution on prescription drug prices that should be expanded to more discounts for more drugs for more people."

In another statement, Merith Basey, CEO of Patients for Affordable Drugs, noted that "Medicare's third round of negotiated prices demonstrates what patients already know: negotiation works. Across two administrations, Medicare has secured lower prices and billions in savings for patients and taxpayers."

Finally, Nancy LeaMond, AARP executive vice president, said, "For decades, AARP has fought to lower prescription drug prices, helping secure the historic 2022 law that gave Medicare the power to negotiate lower prices. Today's announcement is another victory in that fight."

#5515. Toxic Port Pollution Costs Europe €2.5bn A Year In Health & Environmental Damages — Study

New research reveals a single ship emits, on average, as much toxic sulphur at port in a year as 19,300 cars, leaving taxpayers and hospitals to pay the hidden cost of shipping pollution.

Commercial ships docked in European ports inflict €2.5 billion a year in societal and environmental costs, according to new research by T&E. While upcoming EU port rules will cut at-berth damages by 40% by 2030, most vessels remain exempt. Previous research has shown that residents living close to a commercial harbour already face significantly higher risks of cardiovascular and respiratory mortality¹. Tightening port pollution rules would save society billions and protect the health of port communities, says T&E.

Instead of plugging into the electrical grid when they dock, thousands of commercial vessels run diesel generators around the clock to power onboard systems. These idling engines release harmful pollution directly into neighbouring coastal and port communities. Analysis of Europe’s 100 largest ports shows that Rotterdam is the most polluted with costs at €350 million, followed by Antwerp (€220 million), Marseille (€120 million), Hamburg (€120 million), and Genoa (€110 million).

According to the report, removing loopholes in the EU rules would save Europe €1.56bn in health and climate costs. Under current EU rules, outlined in the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR), only large container ships, ferries and cruise ships are required to plug into dockside electricity sockets, meaning oil and gas tankers, bulk carriers, car carriers and other cargo ships are left out entirely. Requirements to connect should be progressively extended to all ship types in the upcoming review to cut emissions and grant ports the necessary long-term predictability.

Eloi Nordé, shipping policy officer at T&E, said: “Port communities are paying the price for ships running their engines 24/7 at port. Fossil fuels only seem cheap because companies offload health and climate costs onto the public. Fortunately, the solution already exists. Plugging ships into shoreside electric power would save society billions and make port cities far healthier to live in.”

On paper, marine fuels appear less costly than drawing electricity from the port grid. However, this is largely because the associated healthcare and environmental burdens are absorbed by the local population rather than ship operators. Once these external costs are factored into energy pricing, generating power from fossil fuels at dock is twice as costly as using shore electricity.

This policy gap creates a lot of planning uncertainty for EU port authorities and electricity grid operators. Without a predictable policy progressively including all vessel types, ports are disincentivised from making long-term investments in green infrastructure, says T&E.

The EU will review the regulation at the end of this year. T&E urges EU policymakers to use the AFIR review to expand shore power to all ships, batteries, and boilers, backed by national port electrification roadmaps before 2032.

Its call is echoed today in a joint letter to the European Commission from the Clean Port Cities (CPC) coalition, uniting industry, civil society, and maritime and energy stakeholders including DFDS and Green Transition Denmark, urging predictable shore power timelines for all vessels, battery charging rules, and faster grid access.

¹ The port-health research cited refers to Mei et al. (2023), “Long-term effects of air pollutants on respiratory and cardiovascular mortality in a port city along the Adriatic sea,” BMC Pulmonary Medicine.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5513. MIT scientists discover a surprising way to boost the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

While we go about our daily activities, the brain gradually accumulates waste, including lactic acid and proteins that are no longer useful. Sleep provides an important opportunity to clear away these substances. As we rest, waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) move through the brain, helping remove waste and maintain healthy brain function.

Researchers at MIT have now discovered a way to make these fluid waves stronger using brief pulses of a gentle sound called "pink noise." When delivered at carefully chosen moments during sleep, the sounds amplify slow electrical waves in the brain. Those stronger electrical signals, in turn, produce larger waves of CSF.

The finding opens up intriguing possibilities for improving brain health. Scientists want to determine whether increasing this fluid movement could sharpen thinking, strengthen memory, or slow neurodegenerative diseases associated with the accumulation of damaging proteins, including amyloid beta.

"We found that we were able to increase the size of the CSF flow wave during sleep, which as far as we know, there hasn't been a method to do before. Now that we can enhance CSF flow during sleep in healthy adults, we're really excited to bring this technology to clinical populations to see what effects we can have," says Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis led the research as senior author. The findings were published in Science Translational Medicine, with Joshua Levitt serving as lead author. Levitt recently completed his PhD at Boston University and previously worked as a visiting graduate student in Lewis' laboratory.

Cerebrospinal fluid is a transparent liquid that surrounds the brain and spinal cord, providing protection against physical injury. It also supports brain function by transporting nutrients, including glucose, and carrying away waste released by brain cells as they consume energy.

In 2019, Lewis demonstrated that functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) could be used to observe the movement of CSF into and out of the brain during sleep. Her team found that this movement closely follows slow electrical brain waves, which are especially prominent during deep sleep.

Building on that discovery, the researchers wanted to understand whether deliberately strengthening these electrical waves would also increase the movement of CSF. Earlier experiments had shown that sounds presented at precisely the right moment could enhance slow brain waves.

"You can make more of these electrical slow waves through an auditory stimulus, if it comes at just the right time. Similar to a child on a swing, if you push them when they're at the right moment in their movement, you can make that swing go farther," Lewis says. "The challenge is: How do you find just the right time?"

To test the idea, the team used extremely short bursts of pink noise, each lasting just 50 milliseconds. Pink noise contains the full range of frequencies that humans can hear, much like white noise. However, its lower frequencies are more prominent, while higher frequencies are quieter. The result is a softer, more balanced sound reminiscent of steady rainfall or a waterfall heard from a distance.

Timing was essential. The researchers needed to deliver each burst of sound when a sleeping participant's slow brain waves reached their peak. To identify those moments, they monitored electrical activity using EEG while simultaneously measuring CSF movement with fMRI.

Combining the two measurements created a technical obstacle. The powerful magnetic fields used in fMRI interfere with EEG recordings, making it difficult to detect the brain's electrical signals accurately and quickly enough to synchronize the sound.

The team addressed this problem by creating a method that removes interference from EEG signals in less than 100 milliseconds. They also designed an algorithm capable of predicting when the next slow wave peak would occur, compensating for the small delay introduced by processing the signals. Together, these advances made it possible to play each burst of pink noise at the intended moment.

Stronger Brain Cleaning Waves During Sleep

The researchers tested their approach in 14 healthy volunteers. They found that the carefully timed sounds increased the size of both the brain's slow electrical waves and the accompanying CSF waves. Importantly, the sounds were quiet enough that they did not wake the participants.

The brain scans also helped explain how the process works. Slow electrical waves were associated with blood vessels narrowing and widening, creating a pumping effect that pushes CSF out of the brain. These slow waves occur during non-REM sleep and become increasingly pronounced as sleep deepens.

By enhancing the electrical waves, the researchers were able to strengthen the fluid movement associated with the brain's natural waste removal process. However, the study did not directly establish whether the stronger CSF waves actually removed more waste or improved sleep quality.

Could Pink Noise Improve Sleep and Help Fight Alzheimer's?

The researchers now want to investigate whether increasing CSF flow leads to more refreshing, restorative sleep, particularly for people who struggle with insomnia. Another major goal is to determine whether the technique can improve the brain's ability to clear harmful substances.

This possibility is especially relevant to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia, which are associated with the accumulation of abnormal proteins in the brain. If stronger CSF movement ultimately translates into more effective waste removal, the approach could offer a new way to address one of the biological processes involved in these conditions.

"Brain waste clearance is really important for Alzheimer's and other forms of dementia, which are caused, in part, by the buildup of molecules like amyloid and tau in the brain. If we can improve brain waste clearance, we may be able to help prevent the buildups of these plaques that lead to disease," Levitt says.

The technology could eventually become accessible outside research laboratories. Levitt has launched a company that aims to develop a home device, potentially in the form of a headband, that would deliver sound at the appropriate moments during sleep to increase CSF flow.

For now, the results demonstrate that a simple auditory stimulus, when precisely synchronized with brain activity, can alter the fluid waves associated with the brain's nighttime cleaning process. Whether those changes can translate into better sleep, stronger memory, or protection against neurodegenerative disease remains an important question for future studies.

The research received funding from a McKnight Scholar Award, a Sloan Fellowship, a Pew Biomedical Scholars Award, the Simons Foundation Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, the MIT EECS Transformative Research Fund, the National Institutes of Health, the Corundum Convergence Institute, and the Panasonic Well Fellowship for AI and Wellness.

#5511. FDA Moves to Boost Drug Quality Testing

— It's important to assess product quality, not just focus on regulatory compliance, expert says

The FDA announced that it's expanding its approach to drug quality testing, combining traditional laboratory methods with newer, faster screening technologies to identify potential problems with medications on the U.S. market. Its Enhanced Approach for Sampling and Testing (EAST) initiative builds on existing surveillance efforts and aims to use testing data to better inform regulatory decisions and inspections, the agency said.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, David Light, co-founder and CEO of independent drug-testing company Valisure, discusses the potential benefits of expanded testing, emerging technologies being explored through the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health (ARPA-H), and why evaluating finished drug products should complement traditional manufacturing inspections and regulatory oversight.

The following is a transcript of this video:

We need to trust but verify. We need to test more.

The announcement, I think overall, is exciting. I think it's more underscoring how important it is to not just inspect facilities and review paperwork and review approvals, but also to test, to actually test the physical products themselves, the quality of the pharmaceutical drug products.

Is it new? I mean ... it's a new announcement. This is a program that builds upon the DQST [Drug Quality Sampling and Testing] program within FDA, which has been going on since at least 2013. So it sounds like this is an enhanced version, which also sounds exciting, leveraging some new, more modern techniques.

ARPA-H launched a program called FASTPASS just a few months ago -- that stands for Fast Assessment of Solutions, Therapeutics, Pharmaceuticals, and Supplies -- effectively trying to scan or test the quality, not just compliance, but the quality of about 70 million shipments of pharmaceutical products into the United States in all U.S. ports every year. That certainly, as they say, is an ARPA-Hard task.

The idea of using modern testing techniques is interesting. I mean, their DQST program is having conventional techniques as the foundation. Looking at a product from many different lenses, many different techniques and methods, I think, is actually really important. I think that's part of what independent testing has shown over the years and what perhaps some of the previous testing programs have missed.

One of the things that I saw that was very exciting in the FDA announcement is that they're talking about this kind of data driving regulatory policy and FDA inspection planning. I think a big part of regulatory testing is essentially seeing if something's legal to be on the road, right? Is it legal to be marketed and sold in the U.S.? And that's regulatory compliance. But what we focus on in independent testing is more of a market driver, what procurement actually looks for, which can be not just, is it legal to be on the road or legal to be sold, what are the best quality products or the lowest risk, but both have an influence on the other.

So I think the two can really overlap very well to help compliance and help with driving the market to a race to the top as opposed to the race to the bottom. But driving the market to a race to the top, to be as good as possible, I think is certainly a key driver of independent testing and quality testing. The two can absolutely work hand-in-hand. I think they do and will hopefully work even more in the future.

I don't have much visibility in what the FDA means by modern testing techniques, faster testing techniques, that they're saying is being done with traditional methods. I assume it may leverage some of the technologies that ARPA-H is looking at as well. ARPA-H is looking beyond the conventional traditional destructive testing where you need to essentially dissolve a tablet or a capsule in a solvent, run it on a mass spectrometer or run it on an HPLC [high-performance liquid chromatography].

These are expensive, lengthy types of tests, which are very, very precise. So can you still leverage insights with a core tenet of ARPA-H project's non-destructive testing? So laser-based approaches, other technologies like terahertz or NMR [nuclear magnetic resonance], NQR [nuclear quadrupole resonance], hyperspectral imaging. One of the core areas that actually Valisure has been developing for over a decade is a Raman technology-based approach, which is laser and looking at what reflects back as a chemical fingerprint of the product. You can actually identify some pretty serious quality issues by doing that.

I think there's been a lot of talk in previous years that you can't test your way into compliance. You have to have a regulatory overview, you have to have product inspections, you have to have a GMP [good manufacturing practice] process that's very robust, which is certainly true, but testing at the same time is very complementary to that. And I think we're seeing more and more evidence of it and more growth in that area.

#5510. Rotterdam’s Methanol Expansion Is Not an Inland Shipping Fuel Strategy

Rotterdam is expanding its methanol and ethanol business for industrial customers and ocean-going ships. Its inland freight fleet needs a different energy strategy. Confusing cargo, marine bunkering and propulsion would commit port authorities to parallel fuel networks when regular freight routes offer a stronger case for direct electrification.

In May 2026, Tankmatch’s inland bunker vessel MTS Experience delivered certified biomethanol and second-generation ethanol to X-Press Feeders’ ocean-going Eco Levant. The fuels were transferred separately and blended aboard the receiving ship into 90% methanol and 10% ethanol. It was Rotterdam’s first ethanol bunkering of a seagoing vessel. The receiving ship burned the alcohol blend. The inland barge delivered it as cargo. Those are two different businesses.

Rotterdam had already announced an expansion of Evos’s Europoort terminal. Five storage tanks totaling 67,500 m³ are planned for methanol and ethanol, along with an inland-shipping berth scheduled for completion in early 2028. The berth includes shore power for vessels alongside. The project expands industrial storage, cargo transshipment and marine bunkering capacity. Developing an electric inland-freight corridor requires a separate charging and battery-service plan.

Low-carbon alcohols have a role in shipping services that still need liquid fuel. Aviation competes for oils and fats suitable for renewable diesel, leaving other sustainable feedstocks for marine alcohol fuels. I reassessed biomethanol’s role in the residual liquid-fuel market and examined alcohol-fuel generators as range extenders for hybrid ships. The investment test is lifecycle emissions, delivered fuel cost and demand from ships that need liquid energy.

The five planned tanks add 67,500 m³ of storage capacity across several markets. Rotterdam’s biomethanol bunkering grew from about 3,900 tons to almost 12,000 tons in 2025, according to the port authority. That is growth from a small base in the wider bunker market. Long-term investment still depends on recurring customers, contracted volumes and infrastructure utilization.

Ocean-going ships arrive with different engines, fuel contracts and routes. International ports will serve several bunker fuels for years. Los Angeles and Long Beach are approaching this market in stages, beginning with the fuels visiting vessels can buy and the commercial commitments needed for expansion. My assessment of those ports makes the same distinction between proving safe delivery and proving repeatable demand.

Inland shipping is a separate energy business. Many freight routes repeat between a limited number of ports and terminals. Charging equipment, onboard storage and battery exchange can follow sailing schedules, cargo cycles and terminal availability. A shared electrical network can serve dry cargo barges, chemical tankers and container vessels with different battery configurations and common interfaces.

My 98-page inland freight electrification report models five complete loaded-and-empty route cycles. A local port-canal shuttle requires 1.8 MWh, regional industrial service 4.3 MWh, irregular service 8.3 MWh, a major-port corridor 13.1 MWh and a long industrial corridor 36.8 MWh. These planning values precede vessel design margins. The twentyfold spread calls for different battery sizes, exchange frequencies and charging arrangements within a common electric propulsion system.

Some predictable services can charge fixed batteries during normal stops. Others benefit from exchangeable 20-foot battery containers, with smaller onboard batteries supplying hotel loads and resilience. Long corridors need reliable intermediate energy points. Hazardous-cargo tankers need cargo-pump integration, electrical segregation, fire protection and appropriate approvals. Those are problems of vessel design, safety approval and electrical infrastructure. Adding hydrogen, LNG and methanol supply chains adds costs of its own.

The Dutch Zero Emission Services model is already operating at modest scale. It lists five charging stations, two vessels in service and twelve conversion subsidies. Battery-container ownership and energy service can be separated from vessel ownership. Its shared interfaces demonstrate how multiple operators can purchase energy service from the same battery and charging network.

The Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine records battery, hydrogen and LNG vessels, then argues that inland navigation has no universal propulsion solution. Its selected deployment database includes passenger vessels as well as freight. That inventory tells us which technologies have been tried. Comparing their economics and infrastructure costs is a separate task. Inland fleets can use varied hulls, battery sizes and charging arrangements while converging on electricity as the main propulsion energy carrier.

Port authorities need three distinct investment cases. Industrial alcohol storage needs chemical customers and cargo commitments. Marine bunkering needs ocean-going ship demand, fuel certification and contracts. Inland propulsion needs route-by-route electricity requirements, grid connections, terminal windows and a dependable energy service. Sharing port land and utilities can lower costs. Confusing the three markets can multiply them.

Rotterdam can expand methanol and ethanol handling while building a common electric backbone for inland freight. The barge carrying methanol does not need to burn it. Port investment should follow the service purchased by each customer.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment examines Rotterdam’s three energy businesses, the different inland route requirements and the investment implications. The supporting 98-page report contains the route energy and vessel architecture analysis.

#5508. Digital Outages Are Rampant All Across America. Is AI to Blame?

Coincidence is not causation, and yet the urge to ascribe causative power to random events is a typically human characteristic. Take the case of the man who snaps his fingers every five minutes. When a neighbor asks why, he replies, “To keep the elephants away.” “But there are no elephants anywhere around here,” the neighbor points out. “See?” the man says. “It’s working!”

Last week, people who rely on Microsoft Outlook to manage their lives suddenly found it was not working properly. The next day, the FAA issued a rare “ground stop” order because pieces of the digital system that air traffic controllers rely on failed.

The following Monday, four of the country’s largest banks found their computer systems were malfunctioning, and United Airlines experienced a computer outage that exacerbated the travails of long suffering passengers still trying to recover from the “ground stop” fiasco. Then on Tuesday, the National Security Agency’s internal communications network went offline, and Apple web services were disrupted.

According to the New York Times, Senator Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, told reporters last week, “I think we ought to be briefed thoroughly on what is actually happening here. If this is all a coincidence, it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.”

The president of the United States offered this reassuring statement: “It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and have all the money, things like this happen. It’s fine.”

Not surprisingly, with all the talk about AI taking over the world and employees quitting their jobs to warn people of the danger, quite a few people are wondering if AI is responsible for all these digital disruptions.

For some Americans, the timing and scale of the outages made it hard to believe that sheer coincidence was the explanation. In a curious way, AI is involved, but not in the way you might think.

Ever since the digital revolution began more than 50 years ago, the computers we depend on have only been able to do what humans tell them to do. Those instructions are created by coders — people who use the programming language of the day that tell computers what to do and how to do it.

It is well known in the trade that millions of lines of bad code exist. It is a phenomenon known as “garbage in, garbage out” or GIGO. Digital firms employ phalanxes of people to check the code their coders write, but it is a tedious process that often misses even glaring errors. Curiously, the most effective way to find bad code seems to be by using artificial intelligence, which can scan 10,000 times more lines of code in a given amount of time than a human can do.

Tech startup Calif said in a blog post this week that, using AI, it had found a critical flaw in Java4Shell, which leaves much of the internet exposed to cyber attacks if it is not corrected. Java is a popular programming language used by most Fortune 500 companies, according to Politico.

“Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems,” Calif wrote. It calls Java “the beating heart of the modern economy.” Oracle, the developer of Java, released a patch for the vulnerability Tuesday. South Korea’s intelligence agency reportedly sent a separate security advisory earlier Tuesday to public institutions, warning them to fix the issue and prevent hackers from exploiting the Java flaw.

The Java vulnerability comes weeks after a separate major vulnerability was discovered in another popular programming language, PHP, which powers up to 70 percent of the internet. At the time, governments worldwide advised organizations to take their sites offline to patch the vulnerability and prevent breaches.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on Fox News that ongoing efforts to patch the PHP vulnerability took an internal National Security Agency communications system offline Tuesday. He added that AI is making it easier to find such vulnerabilities, which can take years to fix without using the power of AI to find them.

Peter Avery is the chief information and security officer for Velocity Security, a cyber security firm in Michigan. He told the New York Times he was skeptical that the events of last week were connected. “I like facts,” he said. “And until now, these are all separate issues.”

Drawing patterns where they do not yet exist, he said, is human nature. It’s part of the need to make sense of things, he said, but can lead down a dark road. “When you start to live in that world where everyone’s a liar and no one is telling the truth, you are starting to live in fear.”

Maybe snapping your fingers every five minutes is our best defense against cyber criminals stealing our data and crashing our online persona. That’s not a particularly comforting thought.

#5507. New York Just Banned Subscriptions For Features Your Car Already Has

In-vehicle subscriptions are pretty universally maligned among car owners. Most folks don't like the feeling of having to pay every month for features their cars were supposed to come with, and now New York State is doing something about it. Governor Kathy Hochul just signed a bill that bars automakers, dealers and their agents from selling subscriptions for features that are already installed.

The new law, which takes effect on February 27, 2027, is part of a new section of the state's General Business Law, according to Spectrum News. You can read the law for yourself here. It lays out fairly simple ground rules when it comes to subscriptions dealers or manufacturers can offer you: The feature must use hardware already in the car when it was bought or leased, and it must keep working without continual costs or support from the automaker or a third party. Those two things pretty much bring an end to crap like subscription-based heated seats and alike. It also is supposed to cover hands-off driving systems and enhanced navigation. Basically, once the hardware is physically in the car and the manufacturer isn't paying anything for you to use it, they can't then charge you. OEMs will also not be able to charge for software updates that fix safety defects.

Hochul called the practice a "deceptive business model," according to CBS 6 Albany. She also told automakers to keep their hands out of New Yorkers' wallets. It passed through the New York State Senate 57-3.

As with all good things, there are some exceptions. First of all, your lease or payment plan doesn't count as a subscription, so don't even try it, slick.

The law also doesn't apply to navigation updates, infotainment features, satellite radio, in-vehicle WiFi, telematics, roadside assistance or "vehicle-connected services" that rely on cellular data or other networks, according to Motor1. It also exempts software-dependent driver assistance features, like Tesla's Full Self-Driving or GM's Super Cruise.

I know what you're thinking. Didn't I just mention that hands-free driving systems are covered? Well, yes, but subscriptions tied to software and data are likely to survive, while hardware-only features are the real targets. Automakers will almost certainly make the argument that things like FSD and Super Cruise are "connected" or "software-dependent."

One prime example of what this bill aims to get rid of is BMW keeping things like a 360-degree camera behind a paywall. That hardware is already built into the car, and, as we reported, it doesn't require a data connection to operate. It's the same thing with features like high-beam assist and remote start, so I imagine it'll be hard for BMW and other companies with similar schemes to argue that these are "connected." I mean, these are the same people who argue that buyers actually want subscriptions, which is certainly not true.

In any case, violators will face civil penalties of up to $250 per point-of-sale for each violation, though it's not clear exactly how that'll be counted. It's not clear if other states are going to follow suit, but here's hoping.

#5505. A hidden biological divide may help explain Alzheimer’s and chronic pain

Emerging research suggests that biological sex and genetics may play a major role in how neurological disorders develop, progress, and respond to treatment. The findings, which will be presented at Neuroscience 2026, reveal important differences that could help researchers develop more personalized approaches to treating complex brain conditions. Neuroscience 2026 is the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience and the world's largest source of emerging news about brain science and health.

Researchers are increasingly finding that certain neurological conditions can behave differently depending on a person's biological sex and genetic makeup. Understanding these differences could lead to treatments better suited to each individual's biology. Two conditions receiving particular attention are Alzheimer's disease (AD), an incurable disorder that progressively damages memory and other brain functions, and fibromyalgia, a chronic illness marked by persistent pain and fatigue that affects 2-4% of the global population. According to the World Health Organization, Alzheimer's affects between 35 and 40 million people worldwide.

Menopause, Genetics, and Alzheimer's Disease

Two of the new studies highlight how menopause and inherited genetic factors may influence Alzheimer's vulnerability and treatment responses.

One investigation found that people carrying genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's responded differently to menopause hormone therapy (MHT) compared with those without the same genetic risks. The effects also varied according to the particular combination of hormones used. These findings suggest that both genetic background and hormone therapy formulation deserve consideration when evaluating treatment options. (Mateja Perović, University of Toronto)

A separate study examined rodents undergoing menopause that also carried genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's. Researchers observed that brain circuits responsible for memory became particularly vulnerable, providing evidence that menopause may represent an important period of increased susceptibility for women who are genetically predisposed to the disease. (Stephanie M. Perez, University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio)

Sex Differences in Chronic Pain and Brain Inflammation

The other two studies explored how biological sex influences pain sensitivity, immune activity, and the effects of inflammation on the brain.

In a mouse model of fibromyalgia, females continued to show heightened sensitivity to touch and stronger immune system activation compared with males. The findings suggest that the biological processes contributing to chronic pain may differ between sexes, potentially making treatments tailored to these differences more effective. (Yasmin Sahlloul, University of Cincinnati)

Another investigation uncovered differences in how prolonged intestinal inflammation influences the brain. Using a mouse model, researchers found that chronic gut inflammation affected brain function and Alzheimer's related disease changes differently in males and females. The results provide additional evidence that biological sex may influence the relationship between inflammation and neurological disease. (Nurcan Kilic, University of North Dakota)

Toward More Personalized Treatments for Brain Disorders

Together, the four studies underscore the importance of examining sex and genetic differences when investigating neurological conditions. By identifying biological factors that influence disease progression and treatment responses, researchers hope to move toward more precise therapies for Alzheimer's, fibromyalgia, and other difficult-to-treat brain disorders.

"These four studies illustrate the fascinating discoveries that can be made when focusing on female-specific biology or possible sex differences in AD-related symptoms and risk factors," said Liisa Galea, PhD, Treliving Family Chair in Women's Mental Health at Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and moderator of the press conference. "The research presented at Neuroscience 2026 helps us pinpoint the specific differences that may help us develop more targeted treatment using precision approaches, even for some of our most complex brain disorders."

#5504. The True Cost of In-Port Emissions

How current shore power rules cost hundreds of millions every year in health and climate damages.

Air pollution and climate emissions from ships at berth impose a heavy and unaddressed burden on European port communities and local economies. While the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation (AFIR) took an important first step by mandating Onshore Power Supply (OPS) for large container and passenger vessels, several blind spots leave over half of all in-port emissions unregulated.

To quantify the cost of inaction, we evaluated at-berth emissions across the 100 largest EU ports using CE Delft’s Handbook on the External Costs of Transport. Based on 2024 MRV data, in-port emissions cost €2.53 billion every year in health damages and climate abatement costs. Covering only the electricity demand from large unregulated ship types would already save €500 million annually, while tackling boilers would save another €714 million. Shipping companies effectively offload these costs onto public budgets, making fossil fuels appear artificially cheap. Once all impacts are counted, using electricity when at berth is half as expensive as burning fossil fuels.

While AFIR successfully kickstarted early shore power roll-out, its narrow scope leaves significant volumes of emissions unaddressed. Beyond health and climate impacts, this partial coverage creates uncertainty and deprives port authorities, network operators , and investors from the predictability they need to develop and deploy the required infrastructure. Providing a clear time horizon for the provision of shore power to all ships is essential to share infrastructure costs, reduce electricity prices and permanently clean up air in ports.

By Eloi Nordé, Shipping Policy Officer, T&E

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.
