With everything else going on in the world at the moment, you'd be forgiven for forgetting that there's an entire trade war happening between the U.S. and Canada right now, but I'm here to remind you that bad boy is still raging. Much of that is thanks to auto tariffs — one of the major sticking points dividing the two North American countries as negotiations heat back up following a last-minute collapse this summer.

Automotive and other key industrial sectors, like steel, are holding up a deal that could end the two-year trade war. President Trump enacted a 25% tariff on auto imports in April of 2025, and Canada came right back with its own in-kind duties soon after. It's a real mess, and it's driving up costs for everyone. Obviously, this didn't need to happen. Trump didn't need to do this, but here we are. From Automotive News:

Both sets of tariffs include exemptions for locally made parts, which lowers the effective tariff rate on Canadian vehicles exported to the United States to about 12.5 per cent and U.S. exports to Canada to about 21.25 per cent — though the exact rate varies by plant and model.

Trump has repeatedly claimed the United States does not need Canadian-made cars and pressed automakers to shift production south of the border. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has maintained that any agreement with the United States must leave Canada with a viable auto sector.

Ottawa has been pushing for a deal that will put the effective tariff rate for Canadian vehicle exports to the United States on an even keel with those built south of the border but has been hard-pressed to get there, [Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association president, Flavio] Volpe said.

As negotiators closed in on a deal this summer by pitching a broader parts exemption, the U.S. offer would have left Canadian autos facing up an effective tariff of up to 7.5 per cent tariffs, he said. While an improvement over the roughly 12.5 per cent rate automakers face today, it is still higher than the industry's profit margin, making it too high for Ottawa to accept, Volpe added.

Canadian negotiators are "not religious" about what mechanism is used to bring the effective tariff rate down, Volpe said, but want to put plants on both sides of the border back on an even playing field.

Counterintuitively, U.S. assembly plants are not immune to tariffs.

Parts compliant with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement reach U.S. assembly lines tariff-free, but American-made vehicles compliant with the trade deal can include 25 per cent parts content from overseas. That content faces up to 25-per-cent tariffs, translating into a tariff rate on U.S.-made vehicles of as much as 6.5 per cent.

A 3.75-per-cent MSRP credit for American-made vehicles offered by the U.S. Department of Commerce — effective through 2030 — offsets part of these added costs.

But even automakers building USMCA-compliant vehicles in the United States can face an effective tariff rate of 2.75 per cent. The tally can be more or less, depending on where companies source their parts.

The five automakers that currently produce vehicles in Canada — the Big Three, Honda and Toyota — are pushing hard for an interim deal that would close or eliminate the tariff gap between Canadian and U.S. plants, even if it's a short-term solution.

Right now, there's no real timetable for when a deal could be reached, though Canadian pundits are actually aware that Trump has threatened to hike tariffs to 50% at the start of 2027. While they don't think it'll happen, with Trump, it can never be truly ruled out.

A former Volkswagen engineer pleaded guilty to insider trading based on secret information he possessed about the automaker's planned $5 billion joint venture with electric vehicle maker Rivian. Michael Stamp pleaded guilty to securities fraud in a Manhattan federal court as part of a deal with prosecutors, confessing that he used his brokerage accounts to buy Rivian shares and options while in possession of confidential information about the merger that he had learned from another employee.

As we previously reported, the 31-year-old and another former VW engineer, Marcus Plank, were charged in July with making a combined $300,000 trading before the Rivian deal was announced publicly. Prosecutors said Stamp made a cool quarter million, and Plank made $50,000 while also passing information to a family member who made $12,000. From Bloomberg:

"I knew that what I was doing was wrong and a breach of my duty to my employer," Stamp said at a hearing before a federal judge.

Volkswagen and Rivian announced the deal on June 26, 2024, giving Rivian a financial lifeline as manufacturers large and small began to rethink strategies in a slowing market for electric vehicles.

Stamp and Plank, who were both living in San Jose, California, while on assignment from Germany, were initially charged with conspiracy and securities fraud and faced as much as 25 years in prison if convicted of the most serious counts at trial. Plank has pleaded not guilty and is free on a $500,000 bond.

Prosecutors said internet searches made around the time of the crimes showed that the two men knew what they were doing was illegal. Just eight days before the announcement, Stamp — that goofus — searched for "statute of limitations insider trading," according to the government. Soon after, Plank's aforementioned family member searched in German "how is insider trading prosecuted?"

Well, big dog, this is how it's prosecuted — unless you're very rich or in Congress.

There's another fun chapter in the war over Stellantis' Brampton Assembly plant in Ontario, Canada. Now, it's spilled over into court as the automaker has filed a lawsuit against the Unifor workers' union, alleging it is impeding an environmental assessment necessary for the sale to defense contractor Roshel to go through.

In documents filed in the Ontario Superior Court of Justice, Stellantis said it is seeking an injunction that would require the union, its national president Lana Payne and Unifor Local 1285 plant chairperson Ardis Snow to stop blocking the Brampton plant and preventing work at the site. The company wants the court to declare that the union has trespassed at the facility and "obstructed the lawful entrance to and exit from the premises." From Automotive News:

A statement of claim said union officials are "physically preventing, impeding, and restricting Stellantis' ability to provide access to the premises" to environmental consulting firm Pinchin Ltd.

Pinchin was retained by Roshel — the armoured vehicle manufacturer that agreed to buy the idled Brampton plant from Stellantis for an undisclosed amount earlier this month — to carry out environmental work starting Nov. 9, according to the documents.

However, Stellantis said that morning, union representatives blockaded entrances to the plant with trucks, pylons and individuals carrying Unifor flags and that Unifor told the automaker it wouldn't let Pinchin personnel or equipment through.

"To date, Unifor has continued to obstruct access by persons associated with the environmental work, and Pinchin has not been permitted to perform the environmental work," the statement of claim said.

"Despite Stellantis' reasonable efforts to obtain police assistance, those efforts have not brought the obstruction of or interference with lawful access to the premises under an acceptable degree of control, nor has Pinchin been permitted to access the premises."

The allegations have not been tested in court.

The statement of claim said Stellantis "is suffering and will continue to suffer irreparable harm and other losses," although the extent of those losses "are extremely difficult, if not impossible, to quantify in monetary terms."

It added that "continued obstruction" of the environmental assessment "threatens to delay or prevent completion of a material diligence step, interfere with the timetable for the proposed transaction, and affect the responsibilities of Stellantis and Roshel following closing of the proposed transaction."

Stellantis' deal with Roshel is expected to close in mid-December, subject to certain conditions, according to the documents.

In response, Unifor said it has been "demonstrating in support of Canadian jobs at the Brampton plant throughout the past year." Payne said that the sale of the plant to Roshel is "unacceptable" to the union, and it will continue to work with all parties to get a different outcome.

Amazon Autos isn't satisfied with taking on just the U.S. automotive industry, so it has turned its attention to the United Kingdom. Early next year, customers in the UK will be able to buy a new car right on Amazon.com. It'll be the first time the U.S.-based e-commerce giant expands its auto services to an overseas market. As it was in the U.S., the first brand to team up with Amazon Autos in this endeavor is Hyundai. From The Wall Street Journal:

With the Amazon Autos platform, customers will be able to browse real-time dealer inventory, see upfront pricing, get an instant trade-in valuation, connect with a local dealer, as well as reserve a car, the statement said.

Hyundai's IONIQ series as well as its i20 and KONA models will be available on the platform. More brands and dealer partners will be announced before its launch.

Around $1.3 trillion of cars were sold by dealerships in the U.S. last year, according to the National Automobile Dealers Association.

Amazon Autos was first launched in December of 2024, and the program has expanded to over 150 cities in that time, and it now sells vehicles from 35 brands. I'd expect a similar sort of expansion in the U.S. in due time.

The neat trick with Amazon Autos is that you can sort of use it how you want to. Some customers use the platform from start to finish, visiting the dealership just to pick up the vehicle. However, some start the process on Amazon and then visit the dealership to apply for financing or finish the process. Amazon may be, uh, bad, but I do appreciate that sort of choice and flexibility.

#5485. As GLP-1 Use Grows, Patients and Doctors Rethink Thanksgiving Dinner

— Navigating the holiday while taking weight-loss drugs

For many people, Thanksgiving can feel like a competitive eating event. But for Kim Dillard Davis, one of millions of American adults who take prescribed GLP-1 receptor agonists, it is a day like any other.

The 54-year-old Raleigh, North Carolina-based digital creator and wellness coach has lost around 80 pounds since 2023 using GLP-1 drugs. Thanksgiving on a GLP-1 means she doesn't participate in the part of the holiday associated with indulgence.

"I can't sit down and eat the amount of calories that I once could. I'll still be able to sample everything, but I just can't overdo it," said Dillard Davis, who said she plans to be on the drug for life so long as her insurance is covering it.

More and more Americans are using GLP-1 agonists, and as the medications become more popular, they could be changing some Americans' approach to food-centric holidays like Thanksgiving, altering how they eat, what they enjoy about food, and scrambling some social interactions surrounding food.

The jump in popularity comes as President Donald Trump's second administration has made expanding access to GLP-1 drugs part of its health policy, arguing that the drugs, if made more affordable, could help combat rising obesity rates and other related chronic illnesses, eventually lowering broader healthcare costs.

While GLP-1 drugs will likely cause major shifts in ways that are hard to predict, Ashley Gearhardt, PhD, a psychology professor at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor, suggests the overindulgence associated with Thanksgiving could diminish over time.

"I anticipate that flavors and tastes that have been culturally linked with Thanksgiving will continue to be important. There just may be fewer turkey comas at the end of the day," she said.

Navigating the Holiday While Taking GLP-1 Agonists

Some people who use GLP-1 drugs feel full faster and stay full longer, meaning they tend to eat smaller portions. The drugs have been reported to change how people think about food, reducing cravings and emotional eating but also diminishing the sensory pleasure people get from food. Some users also avoid eating rich or heavy foods, because the drugs can cause nausea or bloating.

Doctors say people who are just starting their weight-loss journey this year with the drugs should be particularly mindful of potential side effects.

"Thanksgiving doesn't have to be off-limits," said John Horlander, MD, a gastroenterologist in Louisville, Kentucky. "The key is moderation, smaller portions, avoiding excessive fatty foods, staying hydrated, and recognizing warning signs."

"A little prevention can go a long way toward keeping someone out of the emergency room over the holiday," he added.

The Trump administration has framed its steps toward increasing access to and bringing down costs for GLP-1 drugs as "a historic opportunity to reverse the obesity epidemic." More than 100 million American adults have obesity, according to the latest CDC data.

In 2025, Trump, a Republican, signed a deal with drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk to expand coverage and reduce prices for the popular weight-loss drugs tirzepatide (Zepbound) and semaglutide (Wegovy).

And coverage of the drugs for obesity was expanded to Medicare patients this year when the federal government began offering a selection of the brand-name medications to certain Medicare and Medicare Advantage beneficiaries for $50 a month through a new trial called Medicare GLP-1 Bridge. The program is scheduled to sunset after Dec. 31, 2027.

A June analysis by healthcare research nonprofit KFF found that 3.8 million Medicare beneficiaries could be eligible for the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge, based on claims data from 2023. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services does not provide projections of how many people will start taking GLP-1 agonists as a result of the Trump administration's actions. The agency wants to expand access to these treatments, said a spokesperson, who was not authorized to speak publicly and talked to the Associated Press on the condition of anonymity.

Those policy changes come as the share of people on GLP-1 medications for weight loss has risen in the past few years -- 11% of U.S. adults said they currently take the drugs for weight-loss purposes, according to a Gallup poll conducted in May and June. The poll found that 15% of Americans report having used the medicine for weight loss, an increase of 9 percentage points from 2 years ago.

That means Americans, even if they aren't taking the drugs, could find more people on the medication who are sitting across from them at the Thanksgiving table. That could change how people talk about eating.

Gearhardt said that dinner guests should be mindful about not pushing loved ones to eat or commenting on appearances.

"We all have a tendency to kind of monitor and police each other's eating behavior," said Gearhardt, who studies food marketing and how addictive processes shape eating behaviors and mental health.

Commenting on how little or how much someone is eating "usually isn't a great relationship strengthener," she said. GLP-1 users might be especially sensitive, she said, because Thanksgiving can evoke feelings of grief over losing the intense reward sensation of highly processed foods.

Dillard Davis advised family members not to ask, "Is that all you're going to eat?"

"Leave that phrase off the table. We've spent our whole lives overeating. Let us eat small portions and be happy," she said.

Babak Orandi, MD, PhD, an obesity medicine specialist at NYU Langone Health in New York City, said, "There's a social aspect of eating, especially around the holidays. We don't want to lose that."

Patients, Orandi said, should focus "a little bit less on weight loss and a little bit more on weight loss maintenance" during the holidays, so as to not lose the enjoyment of eating.

For Dillard Davis, Thanksgiving has changed in other ways. Because of the reduced appetite brought on by the medication and to avoid large quantities of leftovers at home, her family has spent the last 4 years celebrating Thanksgiving at restaurants.

But as someone who has been on a weight-loss journey since she was 8 years old, she has learned to accept the changes.

"We still have to eat," she said. "Just don't worry about it so much."

#5483. These Are The Non-Car Vehicles You've Crashed

Crashing a car is a nightmare of physics, emotion and bodily injury. The seriousness of the forces involved rarely make for a funny story. Luckily, these stories are not that. Earlier this week we asked you what vehicles you've crashed that were not cars, and it's clear some of you had childhoods built on survivor bias. Well, I, for one, am glad you survived ditching mountain bikes off of mountains and crashing lawnmowers into houses. Not just because you're still alive but, most importantly, you're alive and contributing to Jalopnik. That's right, you're still here for a very good reason.

Unsurprisingly, the Honda ATC makes multiple appearances in the comments section. Those three-wheeled off-roading vehicles are up their with lawn darts in the damage they caused Gen Xers. They were eventually banned in the U.S. because of the carnage. But you don't need to buy a dangerous vehicle to make it dangerous. Other interesting entries: a gas grill, a horse and a homemade go-kart.

Man, they really don't make them like these vehicles anymore, and thank god.

Just remembered the weirdest thing I've crashed.

My dad had some land in West Virginia. There was a tiny river there and it had some very mild rapids that were more of a ford than a rapids, because it was no more than a foot deep. My sister and I would inflate air mattresses and ride them down the "rapids" normally joined by a dog riding a surfboard that was just a piece of foam shaped like one. Most of the time, the dog made the rapids fine, while my sister and I would run into rocks and the like with the air mattresses. Normally after a week of running the rapids, the air mattresses would be completely ruined by running into branches and sharp rocks.

Growing up, dad got a riding lawnmower (Sears 10 hp). Dad morphed it into also being a snow plow with weights on the rear wheels, a homemade plow and a lever to lift and lower it. We had it for years and we took absolutely no care of it other than making sure it had oil before we cranked it up.

One day, it went missing. By this time, it was at peak jank, with a pull starter, blades that never stopped and an uneven deck that was set to dang near chopping up the roots of the grass. It didn't take Columbo to figure how where it was, as we traced a scalped path through many neighbors' lawns and to the river about 1/2 mile away, where the path of 5 O-clock shadow grass ended and the river began. Some drunk teenager discovered that the brake pedal was disconnected, but didn't discover the way to stop it was to drop it into low gear and turn off the engine.

oh jeez, that's a list. Dirt bikes of all sizes, same with quads a trike or two, several flavours of boat including a canoe (that shoal jumped in front of me!) but probably the most memorable, or at least the most story worthy is the scooter my buddies dad rented for us when we went on a joint family vacation to Cancun back in the late 90s.

he rented four, two for me and my friend, one for him and one for the older brother and we went ripping around Playa Langosta the way three teens and an adult that branded himself the 'fun' dad could. Getting progressively dumber and riskier as the afternoon wore on. Eventually as the rental time was running out we decided to make a race of it and I was confident enough after a few hours of pinning that little 50cc Honda that I figured I could lean it like a race bike around a corner.

I could not and luckily came away with it with minimal road rash and a big ol bruise on my shoulder.

The scooter was not so lucky, nor was the magazine stand it slid into. Fortunately insurance had been purchased, unfortunately fun dad was not so fun the remaining days of the trip

I've had my share of mountain bike crashes. The most recent bad one was on a slightly downhill rock field (a bunch of bowling ball sized boulders packed into the trail for 60 feet as a technical feature).

I was going a little too fast, got off the proper line, and went down on my side. Normally this wouldn't be a big deal except rock fields are not very forgiving.

I cracked a couple of ribs which was problematic in that this trail didn't have any short cuts out so I had to ride another 8 miles or so in not very good condition as it was very painful to breathe.

I was sore for a couple months. I also learned to no longer judge NFL QBs who wear flack jackets to protect their ribs. Most painful injury I've ever had. You just have to gut it out.

Back in the '80's my uncle had a farm that I would go work/play on in the summer. My uncle and cousins had just gotten four ATC200 three wheelers that Spring and my cousins and I were all super excited to race 'em all over the farm that summer. I get up there right after school ends and immediately we're off riding through ditches, bombing across fields and having a blast. The big red barn on the farm was at the top of a steep hill with a gravel drive up to and around it. We'd practice to screaming up the gravel drive and as it leveled out, use the negative G-force to whip the tail out into a lurid slide/drift all the way around the barn. On the other side of the barn was the Milking House, so you'd carry the slide between the two buildings with the echo of the screaming 4 stroke bouncing off the walls. Gaining confidence in this technique, we would just continually elevate the speed. First getting air at the top of the hill, then starting the slide later and eventually clipping apexes and throwing gravel everywhere. This abruptly came to an end when I came up the hill the fastest I'd ever gone, got a late start in my slide, went way too wide and clipped the front corner of the milking house on the other side of the barn. The rear axle of the ATC snapped, throwing me over the bars into the side of the milking house and onto the gravel in a heap. This led to the saying in our family, "that boy couldn't hit the broad side of a barn, but sure can nail a milking house!"

I crashed a Honda ATC when I was maybe 11 or 12 years old. Going way too fast in a large horse pasture when I hit a large dip. Flipped me over, and I'm lucky it didn't land on me. Walked away with a black eye and some scrapes and bruises. 0/10 – do not recommend.

Gen X survivor checking in: if you haven't flipped or nearly paralyzed yourself with a Honda 3-wheeler ATC, you're not really one of us.

From Black Mac and cdoggyd and BuddyS and others (so many others)

My dad built me a homemade go-kart with a 5-hp Briggs & Stratton engine. This was no professional shifter kart chassis. It's exactly what you envision when you think "homemade." Only the right rear wheel was powered. We would take it to the local elementary school on weekends because it had a really large asphalt playground out back and no gates. I'd rip laps for a while until I got tired and we'd go home.

I always went clockwise around the lot. Then one day, I decided I wanted to turn left like my heroes in NASCAR. I got a nice lesson in centrifugal force with the powered wheel now on the inside. It pushed me wide and I hit the curb that separated the asphalt lot with the grass field. I did my best Tony Hawk impression as I did a curb grind for several feet on the floor of the cart. What really stood out to me later is that luckily it happened where it did and not the other side of the lot which would have submarined me under a metal bench face first.

There isn't anything that moves I probably haven't crashed. Motorcycles, boats, 4 wheelers, snowmobiles, sleds, coaster wagons, bicycles, wheelbarrows, gas grill, and more. Even hit the house with a lawn mower. I learned a zero steer mower sometimes has "zero" steer on wet grass.

Raleigh Chopper. Tore-off a toenail (riding true 1969 style – barefoot in bellbottoms) and broke a tooth. Good times!

Golf carts are my greatest fear in the world because I watched too many camp counselors drive them like demo derby cars. More than once I saw someone try to do a J-turn on one and roll it over and I was certain I just watched someone die.

#5482. Vitamin B12 may hold the key to treating a rare genetic disorder

A surprising discovery involving vitamin B12 could open new possibilities for understanding and potentially treating rare genetic disorders. Researchers found that the vitamin can correct developmental problems in tiny worms carrying a genetic mutation associated with Verheij syndrome, a rare human condition that causes developmental delays, impaired growth, and short stature.

The findings center on a cellular process called RNA splicing, which helps prepare the genetic instructions cells use to produce proteins. During splicing, unnecessary portions of messenger RNA are removed, and the remaining sections are joined together in the correct order. When this process goes wrong, it can disrupt essential cellular functions and contribute to serious developmental disorders.

Mutations in genes responsible for splicing can cause conditions such as Verheij syndrome. To better understand the effects of these genetic changes, scientists investigated how a related mutation affects growth and metabolism in a laboratory model.

Vitamin B12 Reverses Developmental Defects in Worms

The discovery emerged from experiments involving C. elegans, a tiny roundworm commonly used in biological research. The researchers were initially searching for previously unknown genes that influence lifespan when they began examining a mutation in a gene involved in RNA splicing. The same gene is associated with Verheij syndrome in humans.

Worms carrying the mutation developed problems resembling important features of the human disorder. Their growth slowed considerably, and they remained smaller than normal.

To investigate why this happened, the scientists conducted genetic screens and analyzed the worms' metabolism. They discovered that the mutation disrupted specific metabolic pathways that depend on vitamin B12 and are essential for healthy growth and normal cellular activity.

The researchers then tested whether providing additional vitamin B12 could counteract these changes. Remarkably, the treatment restored the affected metabolic processes to normal and corrected the developmental abnormalities associated with the mutation.

"We were surprised to find that a change in a fundamental process of RNA processing had such a targeted effect on vitamin B12-dependent metabolism," says Jonathan Kölschbach, first author of the study. "Even more exciting was that we were able to largely correct the consequences of this change in the worm model using vitamin B12."

Could Vitamin B12 Help Treat a Rare Genetic Disorder?

To explore whether their findings might also apply to people, the researchers examined publicly available datasets from human cells. They also worked with Hormos Dafsari, a neuropediatrician at the University Hospital Cologne, to collect blood samples from patients diagnosed with Verheij syndrome.

These investigations uncovered evidence of similar metabolic changes in humans, suggesting that the vitamin B12-related pathways affected in the worms may also play a role in the human disorder.

Although the results are promising, researchers have not yet established whether vitamin B12 supplementation can improve symptoms in people with Verheij syndrome. Additional studies will be necessary to determine whether the benefits observed in worms can be translated into a treatment for patients.

The discovery also raises a broader possibility. Metabolic disruptions may contribute more substantially to diseases caused by faulty RNA splicing than scientists previously recognized. Understanding these connections could help researchers identify new therapeutic strategies, potentially extending beyond Verheij syndrome to other rare genetic conditions.

"Our study is a good example of how basic research on model organisms can provide new insights into human diseases," says Adam Antebi, Director at the Max Planck Institute for Biology of Ageing and lead author of the study. "A fundamental biological question can thus give rise to a new approach that could also become medically relevant in the long term."

#5481. Joint Letter on the Revision of the CO₂ Emission Standards for Cars & Vans

Counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford. Manufacturers could meet their targets without selling a single electric car.

Dear Climate and Environment Ministers of the European Union,

We, a broad coalition representing non-governmental organizations, think tanks, energy providers, renewable and cleantech industries, and the e-mobility sector, are writing to express our concern over the current direction of EU discussions on the revision of the cars and vans CO₂ emission standards regulation.

Road transport remains the primary driver of Europe’s oil dependency. This structural vulnerability costs the EU hundreds of billions of euros annually, weakens our economy, and leaves citizens exposed to geopolitical shocks. The second fossil fuel crisis in just four years has already added more than €50 billion to Europe’s energy bill, hitting households and businesses hard.

Our continued reliance on fossil fuels also accelerates the climate crisis. This summer, Europeans paid the price as successive heatwaves brought record temperatures, devastating wildfires, and severe droughts across the continent. Transport remains the EU’s biggest emitter, with cars and vans alone accounting for 16% of total CO₂ emissions.

Yet while the market is moving rapidly, political discussions are falling out of touch with reality.

Europe already has a mature, increasingly affordable and readily available structural solution in electric vehicles – which are also the most effective way to shield consumers from volatile fuel prices. Electric vehicles are scaling fast, reaching a record 27% market share in the third quarter of 2026 in the EU.

Instead of building on this momentum, discussions in the Council on the car CO₂ regulation threaten to slow the EV trajectory and inject uncertainty for companies and consumers. Most concerning is the proposal to create a new category for combustion cars running on e-fuels and biofuels, so-called “vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels” (VEEFs), and count them as zero-emission vehicles.

Too much attention is being paid to combustion-based technologies, distracting from the electric future. Cars running on these fuels still burn fuel in a combustion engine; treating them on par with battery electric vehicles would create a false and unfair equivalence. Under this proposal, manufacturers could meet their targets without selling a single electric car.

Counting combustion vehicles as clean would blur the market signal and bring back the very uncertainty that carmakers, suppliers, and investors cannot afford. It would penalize businesses that are scaling up today and jeopardize the €200 billion already invested in the battery-electric transition. Europe cannot compete globally on electric cars if targets are weakened and undue credit is given to e-fuels, biofuels and hybrids.

We must reset this narrative on vehicle electrification. Europe’s clean industry needs investment certainty and regulatory stability. We therefore call on Climate and Environment Ministers to safeguard the car and van CO₂ targets adopted just three years ago, reject any weakening of the 2030 and 2035 ambition, and remove the “vehicles running exclusively on eligible fuels” (VEEFs) category.

Now is the time for political leadership. Member States have the chance to ensure this fossil fuel crisis is Europe’s last, and to act decisively to build a clean, sovereign, and affordable mobility system supported by a strong EU clean industry.

Download the letter to see the full list of signatories.

Transport & Environment’s (T&E) vision is a zero-emission mobility system that is affordable and has minimal impacts on our health, climate and environment. Created over 30 years ago, we have shaped some of Europe’s most important environmental laws.

#5480. Antibiotic Paste Approved to Prevent Surgical Site Infections

— Bacfenssi becomes the first approved product for local application following colorectal surgery

The FDA approved doxycycline hyclate (Bacfenssi) to reduce the risk of surgical site infections (SSIs) in adults and kids undergoing colorectal surgery, the agency announced on Tuesday.

Sold as a powder to be reconstituted into an extended-release paste, the tetracycline product is indicated specifically for surgeries involving incisions larger than 20 cm, as efficacy for smaller incisions was not established in trials. Pediatric patients must weigh at least 45 kg, according to the agency.

It marks the first approved option for preventing SSIs that is applied locally, the FDA said. Before closing the incision, the paste is applied directly to the fascia and tissues of the abdominal wall along the incision.

Support for the approval came primarily from SHIELD II, a multinational double-blind phase III trial, which showed that adding the doxycycline hyclate paste to standard of care reduced the risk for SSIs, mortality, or surgical reintervention by 40% over the month after surgery. In the investigational arm, that composite outcome occurred in 10.9% of patients compared with 18.1% in the control arm (P=0.004).

When looking at SSIs specifically, a key secondary endpoint, the product reduced the risk by 60%, with infections recorded in 3.8% of the doxycycline hyclate arm and 9.5% of controls (P=0.001).

Commonly occurring following colorectal surgeries, SSIs "can lead to prolonged hospital stays, reoperation, and significant patient morbidity, including wound breakdown and systemic infection," the FDA noted. "Despite the administration of systemic antibacterial drugs prior to colorectal surgery to reduce SSIs, the infection rate remains substantial, underscoring the need for additional preventive strategies."

Adverse events observed in trials of doxycycline hyclate were mostly mild and included incision site reactions, procedural pain, anemia, and wound dehiscence.

Labeling for the antibiotic paste includes potential risks for tooth discoloration and inhibition of bone growth if used in pregnancy and in children, Clostridioides difficile infection, potential for microbial overgrowth, along with known class effects of tetracyclines -- photosensitivity, fixed drug eruption, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic actions. Drug interactions are possible with concomitant use of anticoagulants.

Doxycycline hyclate can cause fetal harm, the FDA noted, and "breastfeeding is not recommended for 40 days after administration."

Launch of the product is expected in early 2027.

#5478. 1971 Chevrolet El Camino With 47,000 Miles Shown Burns Rubber With 454 Big Block And 4-Speed Manual

If you're shopping for El Caminos, then this 1971 example should pique your interest. Listed on Bring a Trailer, the pickup has 47,000 miles on the odometer and features a 454 big-block V8 paired with a four-speed manual transmission. The El Camino in question has been with the seller since 1992 and comes with the build sheet (albeit a tattered one) and a Nevada title.

According to the seller, the 454 V8 was rebuilt and received a replacement camshaft roughly 5,000 miles ago. BaT's description notes that the car's true mileage can't be verified, but that hasn't stopped potential buyers from placing their bids, with the highest bid sitting at $8,500 at the time of writing.

The Fisher body tag shows that the pickup was originally painted Placer Gold. The body, as you can see from the pictures, has since been refinished in red, with black striping on the hood. There are chrome details on the bed rails and wheel openings, as well as chrome bumpers and a drop-down tailgate. Locking pins secure a cowl-induction hood, which was added later. Completing the exterior are 14-inch Rally-style wheels fitted with derby-style hubcaps and wrapped in BFGoodrich white-letter tires.

On the inside, the cabin has black vinyl seats with color-matched carpeting, door panels, and dashboard. And per the Fisher body tag (trim code 706), this El Camino appears to have left the factory with a black vinyl interior. Other highlights include power steering and brakes, a Muncie shifter, a center console, and a Pioneer cassette player.

If you came across this listing earlier, you probably wondered why BaT hadn't listed the car with an SS 454 headline if it was the real deal. There was certainly a lot of activity in the comment section, with doubts surrounding the car's authenticity. Much of the discussion centered on documenting the drivetrain, with commenters coaching the seller on where to find the partial VIN stamped on the engine block.

The more knowledgeable commenters helped resolve the question after the seller posted photos of the VIN stamp on the block, the rear end, and the Posi tag. User ssterry commented, "Congratulations! Photos #129-131 should be more than adequate to convince BaT that this El Camino was born an SS!" BaT agreed, writing in a November 25 comment, "We've reviewed the additional media, and have updated the listing to reflect that the car is an El Camino SS 454."

As you may know, the 454 found its way into a lot of Chevy trucks, including car-based utes like the El Camino. But unlike the more coveted 1970 LS6-equipped models, 1971 SS 454s used the LS5 version of the big-block V8. Even though the LS5 doesn't have the LS6's numbers, the 454 LS5 is still a fairly robust powerplant, rated at 365 gross horsepower and 465 pound-feet of torque (or 285 hp and 390 lb-ft SAE net) for the 1971 model year. Pair that with the four-speed stick, and you have yourself a brilliant excuse for skids and donuts.

The Nevada-based seller appears to be new to the platform. But the comments and the seller's interaction with them have really helped settle the SS question. Get in the mix and place a bid if you're interested. The auction ends on Saturday, November 28.

#5475. Novel ADC Could Be New Option in Recurrent Ovarian Cancer

— A phase III trial will test sofetabart mipitecan in platinum-sensitive and -resistant disease

Promising data from a phase I study presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology congress suggested encouraging activity with the investigational antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) sofetabart mipitecan (Sofe-M) combined with bevacizumab in patients with recurrent platinum-sensitive ovarian cancer.

In this exclusive MedPage Today video, Roisin O'Cearbhaill, MD, of Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City, discusses the early findings and how the three-part FRAmework-01 study could expand treatment options for patients with platinum-sensitive and platinum-resistant ovarian cancer.

Following is a transcript of her remarks:

It was a very exciting phase I study. It was looking at a folate-targeting antibody-drug conjugate, and they were looking at the platinum-sensitive population, patients whose cancer had recurred more than 6 months after prior platinum-based therapy. The majority of patients had measurable disease and they treated the patients with Sofe-M plus bevacizumab. So it was phenomenal to see the waterfall plots with such great response rates, objective response rates, in the vast majority of patients and disease control rates in 100% of the patients.

Not only the efficacy data, but also the toxicity data was very exciting in terms of the thing that we always worry about with antibody-drug conjugates or eye toxicity or pneumonitis. So it was great to see that those really weren't a concern with this novel ADC.

And so based on this and other clinical data, we're actually participating in a global phase III study. There are three different subprotocols in that.

In part A, we're looking at the platinum-resistant population, and that is going to be looking at standard-of-care, single-agent chemotherapy versus the Sofe-M. And then in the other two cohorts, they're for patients who have platinum-sensitive disease. In part B, patients have received a prior PARP inhibitor. And in part C, patients have not received a prior PARP inhibitor. In both part B and C, patients are randomized to the standard of care, which would be carboplatin plus another chemotherapy agent with bevacizumab. And then the investigational arm is looking at Sofe-M in combination with bevacizumab.

I hope that we'll have a new treatment option for our patients with recurrent platinum-resistant and platinum-sensitive disease. It would be really great if we could move away from empiric platinum-based chemotherapy and have other options to offer our patients in the platinum-sensitive setting. And for the platinum-resistant, it would be great to have yet another effective treatment option.

#5473. Tesla's Safety Lawsuits Never Reach Courts Because Of The Fine Print At Purchase

While Tesla faces legal challenges from a who's who of governmental oversight bodies, Tesla has been able to repeatedly dodge private citizens complaints through a seemingly ironclad arbitration clause found in all new Tesla sales contracts.

In fact, civil lawsuits regarding deadly and damaging crashes seem to end in quiet settlement after quiet settlement. When they don't, the payout is massive, like the $243 million judgement after a 2019 Autopilot crash in Florida. So what is Tesla hiding behind closed doors?

The pivotal line item can be found in customer contracts regarding forced arbitration. As the San Francisco Chronicle points out in its investigation, Tesla quietly settled 920 consumer cases in the last 10 years; "twice as many as the nine other top 10 U.S. automakers combined." So far, in the public court records and case logs the Chronicle collected, it found Tesla managed to skirt 12 attempted class action lawsuits because of its ironclad arbitration clause.

Should you find yourself in the unenviable position of buying a Tesla, you'll want to pay extra careful attention to Tesla's Energy Library Knowledge Agent Terms of Use, Full Self-Driving (Supervised) Subscription Agreement, Premium Connectivity Subscription Agreement, and Tesla Assist Terms of Use. All can be read on Tesla's website.

The specific arbitration agreement under each of those sections says that if an issue isn't resolved within 60 days of occurrence, the owner agrees to have any issue resolved via arbitration. Owners are unable to bring about any class-action lawsuits against the company.

Two attorneys found that out when they were hired to take on Tesla. The initial class-action lawsuit they brought against Tesla had 12 individuals behind it which ,due to the agreement, forced it to be broken down into 12 separate arbitrations. And as is the way in arbitration, Tesla wasn't required to supply discovery evidence, especially if it considered any data "proprietary information," so the problem disappeared without any admittance of wrongdoing.

The approach works so well for Tesla that other automakers are beginning to take notice and add similar agreements to their own vehicles or taking cases into arbitration as well. Rivian, also an electric vehicle maker, has already done so.

Owners can at least opt out within 30 days of signing the agreement by sending a letter to a Tesla P.O. Box in Fremont, California. How many of them knew that was a possibility is likely low, as even the Chronicle found most Tesla owners had no idea it was there. To truly see the entire picture you should read the entire investigation by the Chronicle, and watch its accompanying video.

It's a stark reminder of how important it is to read the terms of service to everything you purchase and use before signing. Otherwise, you end up in a losing battle against Tesla, or Stan's unfortunate situation.

#5472. New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

A new wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most important stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.

"This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," said Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up new possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

"REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being."

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD

Building on the initial findings, the research team plans to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a new way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

"Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," said Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need."

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable new tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

Other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

#5471. New Biologics May Be Able to Change the Course of Sjogren's Disease

— Experts discuss promising dazodalibep and ianalumab data presented at ACR

In this exclusive roundtable video from MedPage Today, three rheumatology experts discuss promising new treatments for Sjögren's disease, highlighting emerging data presented at the American College of Rheumatology (ACR) annual meeting.

Moderator Hanna Zembrzuska, MD, of the University of Iowa in Iowa City, is joined by Nancy Carteron, MD, of the University of California Berkeley, and Thomas Grader-Beck, MD, of Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. In this first of four episodes, they examine phase III OASIZ-301 results for dazodalibep and long-term NEPTUNUS extension findings for ianalumab, including whether improvements in salivary flow could signal the potential to preserve salivary gland function.

Following is a transcript of their remarks:

Zembrzuska: Hello, and welcome to MedPage Today Roundtable on the most recent American College of Rheumatology meeting. My name is Hanna Zembrzuska. I'm an adult rheumatologist in Iowa City, Iowa, and I'm joined by some colleagues here who I will have them introduce themselves. Go ahead.

Grader-Beck: Hi, my name is Thomas Grader-Beck. I'm an associate professor at Johns Hopkins Rheumatology. I'm a member of the interdisciplinary Sjögren's center and I'm very excited to be here.

Carteron: Hi, I'm Nancy Carteron. I'm a professor at University of California at Berkeley and UCSF [University of California San Francisco], and I'm based at a Sjögren's center in Berkeley, and I'm happy to be here.

Zembrzuska: Yeah, I'm so happy to be here with Dr. Carteron and Dr. Grader-Beck, and we are going to do a virtual roundtable covering Sjögren's news from the most recent ACR meeting.

This is the most promising era in the history of Sjögren's disease research. For decades, care was limited to managing symptoms like eye drops and saliva substitutes with zero FDA-approved targeted therapies. But over the past year, multiple late-stage clinical trials have succeeded, bringing the first disease-modifying drugs to the brink of approval. So very exciting.

At the recent American College of Rheumatology annual meeting, there was a late-breaking oral abstract session that discussed dazodalibep, which is a CD40 ligand antagonist, and the results from its phase III OASIZ-301 trial. What were your main takeaways from this trial?

Carteron: I'll jump in. I think seeing yet another product meet the endpoints in Sjögren's historically was terrific. I think the fact that it also targets an additional pathway in the disease pathogenesis is promising.

Grader-Beck: I will say one other thing, maybe. I think the side effect profile overall was good. There was a little bit of a signal of hypertension and there wasn't much additional information about that, but maybe that's something to just keep in the back of the mind to see if that is something to really be concerned about. But otherwise, I thought it looked great.

Carteron: I would also add that in their study, they included a pretty significant number of patients that also had another coexistent autoimmune disease. So both lupus and rheumatoid arthritis plus Sjögren's patients were allowed in the study. And I think it was maybe even up to 20%.

I don't think there was any data presented separating that out, but I think that will begin to give us a little more information about real-world use of this particular kind of product. And I think the other point really is it's not a monoclonal antibody, so it's a different technology of inhibition. So it's actually a fusion protein that's very targeted.

But to get to Thomas's point about safety profile, it really does look like the newer technologies have figured out a workaround against some of the thrombotic effects that we saw early on when that particular pathway was inhibited. But intriguing the point that he's making about the hypertension, so stay vigilant.

Zembrzuska: So at ACR, long-term results from the NEPTUNUS extension study for ianalumab were also presented. This study had high retention rates and it reported data on stimulated salivary flow with improvements maintained through week 96. What does this mean exactly? Does this mean that sustained stimulated salivary flow indicates gland preservation or is that too strong of a statement? What do we think this means?

Grader-Beck: Yeah, I mean, it's very, very interesting and it's exciting to see that we see a consistent longer-term signal. So in the extension study, of course, everyone is on the drug and then you have some patients from placebo switching over to drug and you can start to see similar effects in the placebo group in terms of improvement of disease activity. And then also there was a little bit of a signal of the salivary flow.

I think it's too early, it's too early to say. We really need some more dedicated studies to tease that out. But if you look at the more mechanistic studies -- and there was data also presented at ACR this year, and last year actually too -- where you measure, for example, the vascularity in the glands before and after treatment. And you can clearly see a decrease of inflammation if you measure it by vascularity, you can see improvement of infiltrates, you can see actually improvement of salivary flow, but those were not placebo controlled. These are mechanistic studies.

So certainly that all points towards a possible effect. And the way it looks like, it would be patients that are actually earlier in the disease course that have more residual saliva may be the ones that may benefit more.

Carteron: I think we have data showing a decrease in glandular infiltrates of lymphocytes, but predominantly B cells, with deep B-cell depletion from a number of different products looking at it when they have. And so I think the overwhelming evidence is that there can be improvement, and I think even a small amount of improvement in salivary function may translate into a significantly meaningful outcome for patients. Whether it then translates into decreased dental damage or other things, clearly we need more.

But I think that for quality of life, not even well established, but even early on for patients, I find it particularly exciting. And also anecdotally for patients that were within the study that elected to continue and go into the long-term extension study because of a number of factors, but one of them also was increased oral comfort.

#5470. Europe’s Solar Problem Is No Longer Solar

Europe’s solar fleet is delivering. The rules, grids, and investment framework around it are struggling to keep up.

SolarPower Europe’s September mid-year assessment describes a familiar contradiction: solar is contributing more to energy security and affordability, yet weakening policy support, grid constraints, and insufficient flexibility threaten continued growth.

In its September newsletter, the association reported that solar became Europe’s largest electricity source in June and estimated that it avoided more than €30 billion in gas imports for power generation over six months of the Middle East conflict. At that point, it forecast a slight contraction in EU solar deployment in 2026.

Europe’s ambition to become an electrostate is stuck in a State of Confusion and will remain unconvincing unless its rules and networks catch up. The challenge is no longer simply building solar. It is connecting it, using it, and making participation easier.

Ukraine’s September auctions illustrate the shift.

Preliminary results showed that a 50 MW solar auction attracted three bids totalling 38.99 MW. A separate 100 MW solar-plus-storage auction attracted 26 bids totalling 385.9 MW.

The terms differed: price ceilings were €0.08/kWh for standalone solar and €0.12/kWh for solar-plus-storage. These were bids, not completed projects. The results demonstrate stronger participation in the hybrid auction—not proof that adding batteries is inherently more profitable.

Physical projects show the transition too. A September report described Romania’s 918 MWh battery under construction and a separate 120 MWh system commissioned at Teiuș. Bulgaria’s Devnya solar plant expanded from 5 MWp to 65 MWp, adding 60 MW/165 MWh of storage.

But batteries are only part of the equation. Schneider Electric Research Institute’s October system-cost analysis models 40,500 scenarios combining distributed solar and batteries with central generation and networks.

Under global-average cost assumptions, optimised scenarios put total electricity-system costs about 10% below the benchmark, rising to as much as 40% below under assumed 2030s technology costs. These are modelled outcomes, not forecasts of European household bills.

The lesson from this company-sponsored research is coordination: electrifying transport, heating, and industry can improve infrastructure utilisation alongside distributed generation.

Denmark is confronting another bottleneck: access to scarce connection capacity.

Denmark’s October connection-prioritisation reform replaces a simple first-come, first-served approach with categories reflecting societal functions, electrification, and other uses. Within categories, projects placing less strain on the grid can receive priority.

Battery treatment matters. Standalone storage falls in category 3, below renewable generation and electrification in category 2. Qualifying co-located batteries can also fall in category 2.

Storage can increase connection requirements or improve an existing connection’s utilisation. Rules should recognise operation, not merely technology labels.

Europe needs transparent queues, credible project-readiness tests and connection arrangements that reward flexibility—not just faster permitting.

Roofs, station canopies, car parks, and noise barriers already occupy space for another purpose. Adding PV can reduce additional land take, although it does not make generation footprint-free.

Belgium’s Solar Tunnel demonstrates the principle. A 2011 announcement records 16,000 modules installed on a covered section of the Paris–Amsterdam railway near Antwerp, designed to generate 3.3 GWh annually for railway infrastructure and trains.

At Uden in the Netherlands, bifacial PV forms part of an A50 motorway noise barrier. The EU LIFE project’s monitored results recorded 325.5 MWh over 18 months—approximately 220 MWh annually.

The assessment also reports lower-than-expected generation and higher-than-anticipated capital costs. Multifunctional infrastructure is promising, not automatically cheaper. Engineering, procurement, and maintenance determine whether combined benefits justify the premium.

The strongest projects preserve their original function while adding electricity: shade plus charging, noise protection plus generation, or water infrastructure plus power. They complement conventional rooftop and ground-mounted solar rather than replace them.

At the other end of the scale, plug-in solar challenges the assumption that participation requires an owned roof and a substantial installation budget.

Germany’s Federal Network Agency provides a simplified administrative route for qualifying systems, with module capacity up to 2,000 Wp and inverter output up to 800 VA.

Registration remains mandatory. Separate network-operator notification is waived under specified conditions, including the unpaid-export arrangement. These administrative thresholds do not override technical or installation-safety requirements.

Germany’s environment agency explains that qualifying devices within technical limits can be commissioned by non-specialists.

That matters because administrative and installation costs can be disproportionate for small systems. Balcony solar offers a route for people without access to a conventional rooftop installation, including some apartment residents.

It does not replace large-scale generation or remove mounting, electrical-safety, building-consent, and country-specific requirements. Its importance is accessibility: proportionate regulation makes small-scale participation possible.

Europe needs large projects, distributed generation, solar-equipped infrastructure, accessible household systems, batteries, and flexible demand.

Writing from Down Under, the parallel is clear. High rooftop-solar penetration is reshaping Australian daytime demand and electricity prices. The response is batteries, flexible demand, and market rules that reward them.

The choice is not between ambition and practicality. Practical rules are how ambition becomes deployment.

Prof Ray Wills is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.

#5469. Audi Is Bringing Back The RS6 Sedan After A 17-Year Absence

Audi Sport has put out an incredible amount of renowned performance cars over the years, but without a doubt the most beloved by enthusiasts are the various RS Avants. From the original RS2 to the RS4 and RS6, the Avant wagons have far outweighed sedans when it comes to production volume and cultural impact, even if you count the recent four-door RS5s. Some generations of RS4 and RS6 never even received sedan variants, and the last RS6 sedan (the V10-powered C6) went out of production in 2010. That role was filled by the RS7 four-door coupe, and there's no more A7 anymore, either.

For the upcoming RS6 version of the current C9-gen A6, which has been running around testing in camouflage for quite a long time now, Audi is bringing back the RS6 sedan in addition to the Avant. Our spies took a new batch of shots of the RS6 sedan looking even closer to production while testing at the Nürburgring, looking particularly bodacious with its widebody clearly visible despite the camo wrap. To assuage the worries I know are swirling around in your brains, Audi already confirmed the new RS6 Avant will come to America, so the sedan will just be another flavor to choose from if, for some reason, you're someone who hates wagons like those people who say they have an anti-cilantro gene.

This RS6 sedan prototype doesn't have any fake body panels or other earlier-stage camouflage coverings, with the only thing obfuscating the design being the swirly wrap. The new RS5 is wider than a regular A5 by over 1.5 inches, and the same looks to be true for the RS6. Like the RS5, its larger sibling also has a functional vent in the front fenders ahead of the door, and the flared arches are filled with big wheels that look to be 22s.

It's got a similar double-diamond pattern to the wide front grille, and the side intakes in the RS6's front bumper look even bigger than the RS5's. Camo is covering the headlights, which will get RS-specific running light designs and animations. There's a cute little lip spoiler on the trunk, and the rear diffuser has two gigantic oval exhaust tips. The taillights should also have RS designs.

The yellow sticker on the rear window confirms that the RS6 will be a plug-in hybrid, and while early rumors and prototypes pointed to the RS6 using the same twin-turbo V6 as the RS5, we know it will use an updated version of the Porsche-derived V8 that's in the current gas-only RS6 (and that's used in PHEV Porsches and Bentleys). With a large battery pack and an electric motor added on, the new RS6 should have at least 700 horsepower and a usable EV range of a few dozen miles. We'll find out for sure when the RS6 debuts at some point in 2027.

#5467. Hybrids Are a Waypoint, Not the Destination

An earlier version of this article appeared in The Driven on 15 October 2026. This version has been revised and updated with the most recent registration data.

By Ray Wills, Raphael Wellmann, and Peter Newman

In January 2024, Toyota chairman Akio Toyoda said battery EVs would reach at most 30% market share, with the remainder going to hybrids, hydrogen, and combustion vehicles. Norway’s BEV share was already at about 89% that year. Norway alone cannot settle a prediction about the global market, but it shows that 30% is no inherent ceiling on BEV adoption.

PHEVs are conditional transition vehicles. They earn their environmental case through verified electric kilometres, not through the presence of a charging port.

Mature markets tell the more revealing story. Once battery-electric vehicles offer sufficient choice, charging confidence, and competitive economics, hybrids do not settle into a permanent share of the market. Hybrids may lead early, peak, and then retreat.

Norway. The year is 2015. Hybrid vehicles had gained material market share and plug-in hybrids were beginning to arrive in volume. In 2017, PHEVs accounted for about 18% of new registrations. BEV growth temporarily paused, while hybrids benefited from familiar factories, familiar supply chains, and familiar consumer expectation.

After another PHEV surge in 2020 and 2021, the direction changed. By October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 98.8% of Norway’s new passenger-car registrations. Petrol plug-in hybrids represented just 0.2%, and petrol full hybrids 0.3%. Across the first ten months of the year, BEVs held 98% of the market. Hybrids had not become a permanent destination: they had become marginal in new-car sales.

It would be easy to dismiss Norway as a special case: a small, affluent, and subsidy-supported market.

Singapore has a distinctive vehicle-ownership system, built around Certificates of Entitlement, high ownership costs, and tightly managed taxation. Yet its market also shows hybrids losing ground as BEVs expand. Conventional hybrids accounted for 28.3% of new registrations in October 2026, while BEVs held 59.6% and PHEVs 6.2%. The monthly figures fluctuate: hybrid share was higher than in August. The longer-term question is whether hybrids retain their earlier prominence as BEVs become mainstream—not whether their share falls every month.

Denmark provides another example. In October 2026, battery-electric vehicles accounted for 88.2% of all new passenger-car registrations and 97.4% of households’ new cars. The distinction matters: household purchases and the overall market do not electrify at precisely the same pace. But both now show BEVs becoming the dominant choice.

These three markets are not identical, and their policies are not interchangeable. But they show a repeating shape. In leading electrification markets, hybrid share has not settled into a stable plateau. It has risen, peaked and then declined.

For years, Norway was treated as the exception: small, rich, subsidy-heavy, and unrepresentative. But its basic market pattern is now appearing wherever electrification has advanced far enough.

Once the pattern is visible in several unrelated countries, the question becomes whether it is appearing more widely, including in markets still early in the transition.

Trailing-twelve-month registration data across the selected markets show not a world divided between “BEV countries” and “hybrid countries,” but markets at different stages of electrification and following different routes.

Some move relatively directly from combustion vehicles to BEVs. Others pass through a stronger hybrid phase, then a PHEV phase, before BEVs become dominant. In China, PHEVs and range-extended EVs have gained strength alongside BEVs, supported by rapid product cycles, intense domestic competition, expanding charging networks, regulatory settings, and strong domestic manufacturers.

This is not a claim that hybrids have already peaked everywhere. Across the European Union, BEVs accounted for 23.4% of new-car registrations in the first ten months of 2026, while hybrids remained a major part of the market. In Australia, the hybrid share is still close to its high, but in October 2026, BEVs overtook hybrids on a trailing-twelve-month basis for the first time (18.5% vs. 17.6%). The transition remains uneven across countries, buyer types, and vehicle segments.

The route differs. The starting point differs. The pace differs. The picture that comes out isn’t “some countries like BEVs, others like hybrids.” As BEVs meet more buyers’ needs at competitive cost, hybrids face increasing pressure on their share of new-car sales. Whether their absolute sales also fall depends on the size and growth of the market.

There is a practical implication for buyers. A hybrid purchased today in a market that has not yet reached its tipping point may face greater residual-value risk when it arrives on the used market. If new-car demand shifts rapidly towards BEVs while used supply reflects today’s hybrid-heavy sales, resale values may come under pressure.

Fuel prices, tax settings, used-BEV supply, charging access, and export markets will impact, but it is a risk buyers, fleets, and financiers should acknowledge.

If the pattern is visible in the data, why does public discussion so often present hybrids as a permanent pillar of the future vehicle market?

One reason is that the transition is uneven—the future is here, it’s just not well distributed yet. In many countries, people have only seen the rising half of the hybrid curve. The peak and decline have not yet arrived. It is easy to mistake “still growing” for “here to stay.”

Another is that manufacturers with decades of investment in combustion and hybrid platforms have commercial reasons to extend the life of those systems. That behaviour seems rational. Hybrid platforms preserve familiar engines, suppliers, dealer servicing, and factory investments.

But that commercial logic is not evidence that hybrid demand will remain durable once BEVs can do the same job more effectively. As with everything, the biggest cost may come not in going too fast, but in going too slow.

It is also important not to overstate the case against PHEVs. A PHEV that is routinely plugged in can cover much of its owner’s daily driving on electricity. The problem is that many of those PHEVs are not used that way.

European Commission data from 320,000 PHEVs first registered in 2021 found real-world CO₂ emissions averaging 3.5 times their official type-approval values. The Commission concluded that these vehicles were not being charged and driven electrically as frequently as assumed in laboratory testing.

Company vehicles are a particular problem. Petrol may be employer-paid, immediate, and simple to use, while home charging is paid by the employee, workplace charging is unavailable, and reimbursement is cumbersome. Under those conditions, the petrol engine becomes the default.

A PHEV is a bridge—but only if people use it to cross from the petrol side to the electricity side.

The registration data do not say that every hybrid buyer has made the wrong decision. Some households and fleets still need a transitional option. Some regional, towing, remote-area, and high-kilometre uses remain difficult for today’s BEV models and charging networks.

But those are specific use cases that are not representative of the mass market and thus not a reason to preserve combustion systems for everyone.

Conventional hybrids reduce petrol consumption, particularly in stop-start urban driving, but every kilometre still depends on fuel. PHEVs can replace a substantial share of petrol with electricity, but only if they are regularly charged, have enough real-world electric range, and do not unnecessarily run their engine.

BEVs eliminate routine petrol use and are the most energy-efficient option for the expanding share of households and fleets whose driving and charging conditions suit them.

The role of policy is not to pretend that all drivers are identical. It is to make electric driving easier: reliable charging at homes, apartments, workplaces, and regional routes; electricity reimbursement as straightforward as fuel reimbursement; and real-world reporting of petrol use and electric kilometres in PHEV fleets.

The market is not likely to move from combustion to BEV in exactly the same way everywhere. But as battery-electric vehicles become cheaper, more capable, and easier to charge, the addressable market for hybrids contracts.

Hybrids can help drivers transition from the combustion era into the battery electric era.

But that is all they are, a waypoint towards an electric future.

Ray Willis is a Perth-based energy futurist and director of Future Smart Strategies, and Adjunct Professor at The University of Western Australia, who writes on renewables, electrification, and the energy transition.
