#5465. At $17,000, Would You Say The Price Is Right For This 1973 V8 Chevy Vega?

According to its ad, today's Nice Price or No Dice Vega was once a door prize on the TV game show, "The Price Is Right." Today, it appears nicely restored and has a surprise SBC under its hood. Let's see if any of you are game to pay its asking price.

A common way to describe avoidance of an object or idea is the phrase "I wouldn't touch it with a 10-foot pole." The origin of this idiom remains unknown, but a similar, earlier phrase, "not to be handled with a pair of tongs," carries the same meaning. In 18th-century Great Britain, 10-foot was frequently substituted with "barge," as barge poles were typically long and thus offered reasonably remote poking opportunities.

I bring this all up because, based on the comments, the 2017 Alfa Romeo Giulia we looked at on Wednesday was a car that some of you wouldn't touch with a 10-foot pole. That was because the car—and Alfa Romeo in general—carries a reputation for frustratingly frequent breakdowns and bank-account-bruising repairs. That being said, our Giulia's great looks, seemingly good condition, and $7,999 asking price proved a winning combination in the end. That's shown by the 70% 'Nice Price' win it received in the vote.

While not as good-looking as yesterday's Alfa, the 1973 Chevy Vega notchback that stands before us today is an arguably handsome, well-balanced design. The car's mini-Camaro nose and pleasing profile were the best things about it when it launched in 1970. Pretty much everything else about the car, however, was snake-bit from the start.

Chevrolet introduced the Vega in late summer 1970 as the brand's new compact car, nominally replacing the Corvair, which had ended its production run a year earlier. Like the Corvair, the Vega was a clean-sheet design, sharing little carryover parts from other GM cars. Also like the Corvair, the Vega proved problematic for the brand.

The issues that plagued the early model years weren't limited to engineering or production mistakes; even the car's innovative transportation method—shipping it vertically on specially designed train cars—caused unforeseen fluid leaks before the Vegas even reached a dealer. Premature corrosion was another Vega bugaboo, especially in rustbelt states. The biggest problem, though, was with the Vega's SOHC 2.3-liter four-cylinder engine. Built with an alloy block and cast iron head, the engine had no cylinder liners or special wear-resistant coating to keep the bores intact. Chevrolet had to issue recalls on almost every Vega produced to address safety and drivability issues after only two years of production.

Fortunately, someone has addressed at least the engine issues with this Vega by sending its original motor to the recycler and replacing it with a 350 cubic inch small-block Chevy V8. Could there be a more reliable engine than the tried-and-true SBC?

That engine looks right at home in the Vega's engine bay and sits unencumbered by unnecessary ancillaries like a power steering pump or an air conditioning compressor. It does have a heater hookup and a larger-than-stock radiator to cool the plus-size engine. Other engine bay items of note include an MDS distributor and coil and a custom brazed-together air intake that flops the filter over one rocker cover.

Based on the underneath pictures, the V8 feeds what looks to be the Vega's Opel-sourced four-speed manual gearbox and punky factory rear end, so don't expect dramatics at the drag strip out of this car. According to the ad, the car has around 90,000 miles on the clock, but only a couple thousand of those were added after the engine swap. The seller claims it " Drives great and turns heads."

A new engine isn't the only update this Vega has seen. At the same time as the heart transplant, this car also got new candy-apple red paint and fresh vinyl seat upholstery. The remaining original parts of the interior—door cards, dash, and carpets—all look to be in suitably good shape. Two cracks, oddly at exactly 12 and 6, mar the factory two-spoke steering wheel, but shouldn't affect its use or safety. The only other potential misstep is a modern stereo head unit that spoils the overall old-school aesthetic.

On the exterior, all the chrome shines nicely, and the paint appears to be a professionally applied respray. A set of Minilite-esque alloys underpins, and they appear to have reasonably new rubber. As is typical of Facebook Marketplace ads, the ad doesn't mention the car's title status, but given how old of a car it is, we might be able to overlook that.

As noted, the ad claims this Vega had a run-in with Bob Barker on the daytime TV game show "The Price Is Right." Amazingly, that show gave away a ton of Vegas, though a quick search of the videos I could find from the era didn't turn up any featuring this particular car. We'll just have to imagine that experience, along with the opportunity to win a Tappan range or an all-inclusive seven-day adventure to Bali.

Once we're done with all that, we'll have to come back to reality and decide whether this V8 Vega is worth its $17,000 asking price. Yes, no one would have guessed that on The Price Is Right, but that's what makes this an even more exciting opportunity.

What do you think? Is this refreshed, re-engined Vega worth $17,000 as-is? Or for that price, would you refuse to "come on down!"

#5464. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

Researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

The results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the new findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk

To investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

This distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

Moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

However, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

The contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

"Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen said. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk."

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen said.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several important limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

Alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an important distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

For now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

#5463. Plug-in Solar UL Certification for US Safety Regs — What UL 3700 Does & Doesn’t Say

Millions of renters, apartment residents, and condo owners can’t put solar on a roof they don’t control. Plug-in solar, also called balcony solar or plug-in PV, offers a workaround: one or more panels connected through a microinverter to an ordinary wall outlet, with no roof work and, in a growing number of states, no utility interconnection application — though, this is only applicable in select states (users should refer to their state laws before installation). A new safety standard, UL 3700, is helping this market mature, and it comes with a lesson every buyer should learn: a compliant component is not the same thing as a certified system.

Rooftop solar assumes you own a roof, can afford a large upfront cost, and can wait through permits and installation. Plug-in solar flips that. States are responding. As of mid-October, ten states had enacted plug-in solar laws: Utah, Maine, Virginia, Colorado, Maryland, New Hampshire, Connecticut, Vermont, New Jersey, and California. Effective dates vary, with several laws not taking effect until 2027, and New York’s SUNNY Act is awaiting the governor’s signature. Several of these laws require kits to meet a recognized safety standard, and some name UL 3700.

UL 3700, the Outline of Investigation for Interactive Plug-In Photovoltaic Equipment and Systems, was published in December 2025, and UL Solutions began certifying products to it in January 2026. It exists because rooftop solar standards weren’t written for equipment that homeowners plug in themselves. The safety problems are specific:

Hoymiles says the HiFlow Pro was built around these challenges and shuts down in 135 milliseconds if it’s unplugged or the grid fails. For comparison, Maine’s law requires shutoff within 0.2 seconds.

Here is the part that matters most for buyers. UL 3700 evaluates a complete system: the microinverter, how it connects, relevant accessories, and the overall configuration, not the microinverter alone. That means compliance for one part doesn’t automatically establish that the whole kit has been certified.

The HiFlow Pro shows how this works in practice. Hoymiles describes the microinverter itself as UL 3700-compliant, and it has been widely reported as the first plug-in microinverter in the US to reach that point after its July 15, 2026 launch. The complete HiFlow Pro system has not yet finished certification. Hoymiles says it is pursuing it and expects the process to wrap up in December 2026.

The HiFlow Pro is a plug-in microinverter, so the panels are bought separately or as part of a kit. Per Hoymiles, up to four units can run on separate outlets for up to 1,200 watts, depending on state and local rules, and models range from 360 W to 500 W to fit different legal limits. The company lists a peak efficiency of 95.5%, a NEMA Type 6 enclosure, an operating range of -40°F to 149°F, a 12-year standard warranty, and monitoring through the S-Miles Home app. It also cites 250,000 hours of reliability testing, and says TIME named the product one of its Best Inventions of 2026.

Follow the manufacturer’s instructions. Plug the unit directly into a wall outlet, not a power strip or extension cord, and use a GFCI outlet if you’re running a larger system on one circuit.

Hoymiles estimates up to 721 kWh a year from a single 360 W unit, modeled at 5.6 peak sun hours a day and about 2,403 kWh from a four-unit system. At 38 cents per kWh, a rate found only in the highest-cost regions, the company estimates savings of up to about $247 per unit per year and a payback of roughly two years. By our math, that figure assumes about 90% of the power gets used inside the home. Actual savings depend on how much electricity you use during daylight hours, and surplus power may flow to the grid without credit unless your utility offers net metering.

For context, EnergySage puts typical savings from a plug-in kit at $13 to $20 a month at the national average rate of about 18 cents per kWh, and $40 to $50 a month in high-rate states like California, New York, and Hawaii. Two limits are worth knowing: the system reduces your bill but doesn’t replace the grid, and it won’t provide backup power in an outage. The federal homeowner solar tax credit also ended on December 31, 2025, so payback estimates shouldn’t assume one.

Rules vary by state, and sometimes by utility. Hawaii, with some of the country’s highest electricity prices, isn’t among the ten states with a plug-in solar law, so renters and condo owners here should check with Hawaiian Electric and their association before buying. Even in states with laws, utilities may ask for notice, and landlord and HOA protections differ.

#5461. Seabed Mining Has a Refinery Problem Worth Billions

The Metals Company wants to recover polymetallic nodules from the seabed and sell the nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese they contain. That business needs an industrial processing system before its revenue projections become sales. TMC’s November 2026 update exposed the timing problem. Its proposed refinery complex in Brownsville, Texas, may not be operating when offshore collection begins. An established Japanese smelter operated by Pacific Metals, or PAMCO, is the prospective initial route, but it needs modifications to accept commercial volumes of nodules.

That gap belongs in the mining economics. TMC’s 2025 prefeasibility study allocated $4.426 billion to two proposed US hydrometallurgical refineries, about 89% of the study’s $4.971 billion of initial project capital. The denominator has a particular financing structure: the offshore amount covers the first collection system after an Allseas capital credit, while later systems are to be supplied through contracts and paid for through operating costs. The newer Brownsville proposal also has a different industrial scope. The 2025 figure shows the size of the processing business TMC’s economics must support, not a completed financing commitment for Brownsville.

Offshore collection gets the attention. Refineries decide what saleable material a collection system produces and who captures its value. A nodule delivered to port is a complex mineral feedstock, not a sale of four finished metals. One processing route smelts nodules into a nickel-copper-cobalt alloy and manganese silicate, converts the alloy into matte and refines the matte into marketable metals or chemicals. The manganese product needs customers or additional treatment. Each step consumes capital, energy, reagents, skilled labor and working capital.

TMC has a meaningful metallurgical program. Its third-quarter 2026 SEC filing describes earlier North American tests of about 70 tons of nodules and a 2,000-ton industrial demonstration at PAMCO’s Hachinohe facility. Further work at SGS in Canada tested the refining of intermediate material into battery-grade products. PAMCO has completed feasibility work on treating roughly 1.3 million wet tons per year through a modified existing facility. That is a stronger starting point than a conceptual processing flowsheet.

The November 12 corporate update nevertheless put the industrial dependency in plain view. TMC’s preferred Brownsville facility will be difficult to complete before the first commercial nodules arrive, and the Japanese facility requires modifications and aligned schedules. Korea Zinc, Glencore, Hatch, Mariana Minerals and other partners provide useful expertise and commercial relationships. Those relationships still leave the construction, commissioning, financing and refining arrangements to complete.

The value gap matters as much as the capital bill. In our 2025 seabed mining techno-economic assessment, metallurgist Lyle Trytten and I calculated a $553-per-ton contained-component reference value for representative Clarion-Clipperton Zone nodules at fixed historical metal prices. Using estimated purchase terms informed by analogous mineral markets, the same assessment gave a modeled raw-feed value of $188–256 per ton, or about 34–46% of that contained reference value.

The gap pays for real industrial work. Processors bear metal recovery losses, treatment costs, plant capital, financing, product quality and operating risk, and they need a return. The values are estimates on a common reference basis, not bids from refineries or the profit a processor would pocket. Commercial nodule tonnage is often reported wet; TMC’s study assumes 28% moisture. Feed-price comparisons with wet-ton mine costs require the same mass basis.

The mining company has three main choices. It can sell the raw nodules at a price a processor can afford. It can keep title to the material and pay a plant to process it, provided the contract sets capacity, treatment charges, recoveries and risk allocation. Or it can finance and operate refining facilities and pursue a larger portion of the finished-metal revenue. None transfers the work, capital and risk out of the industrial system.

TMC’s own operating estimates reinforce that point. The 2025 study projected $13.622 billion of lifetime processing costs and $3.254 billion of refining costs, together about $103 per wet ton, or 42% of its modeled operating expenditure. Those costs sit alongside the proposed refinery capital. The production system may be offshore, but the economic center of gravity reaches well into the onshore industrial chain.

Impossible Metals has a different, less developed processing position. Its published strategy begins with outsourcing to modified plants in allied countries and envisions dedicated facilities later. Its economic model used approximately $791 per ton of contained-metal value under its selected prices and grades, deducted a $230 processing charge, and arrived at roughly $560 per ton delivered to port. Those numbers use different input assumptions from our assessment and cannot be treated as a direct comparison with the $188–256 estimate. The commercial question is whether a processor would accept the feedstock and the risks on the terms in Impossible Metals’ model.

Existing nickel-processing projects offer warning enough. Ravensthorpe, Goro and Ambatovy had familiar metallurgical technologies yet encountered expensive commissioning and operational difficulties. An unusual feedstock, high-volume throughput, uncertain manganese outlets and synchronized offshore and onshore ramp-up add challenges for nodule ventures. Demonstrating that the chemistry works settles only one part of the investment case.

TMC has considerably more testing and more developed partners than Impossible Metals. That distinction matters. Neither has demonstrated a fully operating processing chain that delivers the required metals at its intended scale, recovery, capital cost and commercial terms. Government financing could change who carries part of the risk, but not what must be built or operated.

A seabed mining company cannot book finished-metal economics while making the refinery somebody else’s problem. Investors, taxpayers and prospective processing partners need to know who provides the billions in capital, who carries the ramp-up risk and how much of the metal value the collector retains after every participant has been paid.

My full TFIE Strategy Briefing article follows the processing alternatives, TMC’s Japanese and US plans, Impossible Metals’ outsourcing assumptions, and the resulting revenue and investment gaps. It is the third article in a five-part seabed mining assessment.

#5460. These Are The Automakers You're Most Thankful For

Happy Thanksgiving! Why are you reading Jalopnik instead of hanging out with your family? They never see you, you know. You barely even call. How bad could one holiday really— oh, woof. That bad, huh? Well, okay, you can hide out in the bathroom a little longer. Don't worry, I'll keep you company with a nice long blog about the automakers our readers are most thankful for.

Earlier this week, I asked you all for the automakers you've been most thankful for over the past year. Today we're looking through your answers, from Mazda to Audi to Smart. About a million of you suggested Mazda, actually, but you can't all end up in the blog. I'm sorry. We're going for a broad range of brands here, so you've got some unique things to think about while you hide away from the political arguments happening over the dinner table. Good luck with that.

Mazda, for the last decade and a bit they're the only brand that tried to inject fun into everything they made. Sure they didnt have a dedicated sports car outside the Miata, and sure they didnt pile up numbers and records for performance but everything from the 3 to the CX9 was on the spirited side of the coin for the segment.

Not to mention they offered, general, affordability without sacrificing options or comforts

Lexus. My daughter got a job at a Lexus dealership as the Delivery Specialist nine and years ago. Two years later I co-signed for her to lease an NX 300 through an employee lease bonus program. She never missed a payment and three years later leased an NX 350 by herself, having built herself a solid very good credit score. And since then, she's leased a third one. She also was promoted to Customer Relations manager in '22, which she still is to this day. I started working at the same dealership six years ago. It's an excellent dealership network and an excellent product. It's been very good for my career as well. But the best part is watching my daughter go from Job to Career under the same roof, we're both managers in departments that work side by side. So I have a great deal of gratitude for the brand. Plus I leased an NX 350h for my wife, it kept her very safe during a head-on collision (low/mid speed, but still). Very grateful for the rigidity

My VW Bug got me into working on cars, and pushing them to their limits (it's more fun to drive a slow car fast than a fast car slow). But these days it's all Audi. The one who started it all with QUATTRO! Owned many and great cars to fling around in the snow.

For me Alfa Romeo. I mean who else has spent so many decades building beautiful, often affordable cars. There's just something when you look at them that other cars don't have.

Smart. It was the first automaker I was truly invested in as a teenage car enthusiast. I fell in love with them at 15, and by the time I was 16, I could practically recite the car's brochure to you. It was the car that taught me that, to be a car enthusiast, you weren't required to love the latest Ferrari or Lamborghini. What you love is what you love. I probably wouldn't be the car person I am today if it weren't for that brand.

This year it's Toyota. This has actually been one of the few periods in my life where I haven't owned a Honda. My 5th gen 4R has been pretty rock solid. I'm going to have to do the belt, plugs, and a few other things soon but that's due to 100k miles. I'm thankful for the forward facing V6 making my life easy to replace those items.

Small companies like Rivian and maybe Subaru who still think it's important to build cars people want to buy and work for your business. Big companies like GM, Ford and Tesla just want to impress investors with quarterly profits with little regard as to what people need or want

What I am thankful for is that they have shifted the conversation.

For at least a decade, the conversation has been. "This vehicle can do more than any other vehicle. Sure costs more, but don't you want the ability to tow the Titanic through the Darien Gap while surrounded by unicorn leather and listening to a 98 speaker 10,000 watt system?"

Then Slate says "Hey it's cheap. Maybe that's not enough for you, but it's enough for many and it's a lot more affordable."

Ford has already responded with the Fathom. I expect other manufacturers will also respond with less expensive offerings that are lower in capabilities and luxuries, but still might be a good fit for people.

So, although I am unsure if Slate will survive and thrive, I am thankful that the conversation of what makes a good vehicle has shifted from crap most people don't need to a focus on what they actually need.

Fiat. For providing long time ago my favorite all time car, the Fiat X1/9 but also putting a smile on my face since 2012 with the Abarth 500!

I concur with Honda and the Prelude – it's such a nice looking coupe.

But, for my obsession of the year, I have to say American Motors. I bought an Eagle this year and my deep dive into all things AMC has earned them very much respect in my eyes.

#5459. Hepatitis B Shot at Birth Dips Among Babies of Infected Moms

— "Birth dose vaccination serves as a critical safety net," researchers say

Fewer newborns are receiving the birth dose of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine, including those born to infected mothers, according to a national retrospective review.

For over 1.3 million U.S. infants born between January 2018 and June 2026, vaccination rates were 76.4% in 2018 and 79.8% in 2022 before beginning to fall in mid-2023, landing at 65.6% in June of this year, reported Nina Masters, PhD, MPH, of Truveta in Bellevue, Washington, and colleagues in NEJM Evidence.

From 2018 through 2025, a positive maternal HBV test led to vaccination in 97%-98% of newborns born to those mothers -- but that percentage dropped to 93.9% during January through June 2026.

Overall, as newborn HBV vaccination rates fell, maternal HBV screening rates rose. Over the study period, 90.5% of mothers had evidence of an HBV test, with 0.18% testing positive for the virus. The proportion of moms who had no recorded HBV test during pregnancy dropped from 15.6% in 2018 to 7.6% in 2026.

"Hepatitis B birth dose vaccination serves as a critical safety net against gaps in protection against perinatal HBV infection," Masters and team wrote.

"Applying the 90% screening rate found in this study to the approximately 3.6 million births per year, mothers without evidence of HBV screening during pregnancy may give birth to an estimated 360,000 infants per year," they noted. "Applying the 0.18% ... positivity rate in this study could translate to more than 640 infants a year born to mothers with HBV infection who are untested."

Universal HBV vaccination of newborns at birth has been shown to be safe and effective. However, the CDC's revamped Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices last December abandoned more than three decades of U.S. vaccine policy and voted to stop recommending a universal birth dose.

The panel recommended instead a shared clinical decision-making process for babies born to mothers who test negative for HBV. Under that approach, parents and clinicians would decide "when or if" to administer the vaccine. For families that opt to not give the birth dose, the panel suggested delaying the first dose until a child is 2 months old. The CDC's proposed childhood immunization schedule would move HBV vaccination to shared clinical decision-making except in high-risk groups.

The steady declines in newborn HBV vaccination rates across all maternal groups "potentially indicate distrust of medical interventions even beyond recommendations," Masters and team cautioned. "These results reinforce previous reports, likely reflecting continuing vaccine hesitancy and confusion among parents after recent changes in recommendations for newborn HBV guidelines."

The trends seen in this study could lead to more chronic HBV infections in the years ahead, according to a recent modeling study. That research predicted that moving from a universal birth dose to deferred vaccination or a shared decision-making approach could increase chronic HBV infections by 19% with delayed vaccination and 83% with shared decision-making. Other research has suggested that unvaccinated infants may face unexpected HBV household exposure risks even when moms test negative.

For this study, Masters and colleagues reviewed electronic health records from the nationwide Truveta Data database. The analysis included 1,338,961 infants born to 1,075,767 mothers who were ages 15-49 years at delivery.

Over the study period, 75.9% of newborns received HBV vaccination within 1 day of birth.

Vaccination rates were highest among babies born to moms who tested positive for HBV, at 96.9%. Vaccination rates were 75.9% among those with mothers who tested negative, 76.8% among those with moms with unknown infection status, and 75.4% among those with moms who had no evidence of a test in the database.

Among the 2,231 mothers who tested positive for HBV infection during pregnancy, 92.8% received both hepatitis B immunoglobulin and HBV vaccination.

#5458. 1965 Plymouth Belvedere 1 Shows 81,000 Miles, Conceals 588 Cubic-Inch Hemi Routed Through Stout Torqueflite Automatic

Like a lot of cars on Bring a Trailer, this 1965 Plymouth Belvedere I has been for sale on the site before. It's up for bid on Bring a Trailer again, but back in 2020 it was bid up to $26,500 without meeting its reserve. According to the present listing, the car was sold privately in 2023. It was modified before 2010 to have a bored 588-cubic-inch Hemi with dual four-barrel Holley carbs.

That engine swap is said to be in tribute to what this car is not — an original A990 Belvedere. Those were limited-run, extra-lightweight stock racer factory builds designed for the capability of a drag car, but legal for the street. According to Hagerty, although the A990s had street-legal accoutrements such as turn signals and mufflers, they also came with a warning label inside their glove compartments that read: "This model is intended for use in supervised acceleration trials and is not intended for highway or general passenger car use."

The thing is, the Bring a Trailer car may be special, but the 9.6-liter V8 stuffed beneath its fiberglass hood isn't what the A990s ran, even paired with a period-correct Torqueflite three-speed automatic. Coronet and Plymouth Belvedere A990 sedans had 426-cubic-inch Hemi engines. They also got aluminum heads and higher compression. At least the dual four-barrel Holleys on the BaT car emulate what the A990s got. Still, this hat-tip-to-history Belvedere is unique, thanks to a litany of mods we'll partially tabulate here.

The Belvedere didn't make our cut of nine classic Plymouth models and what they're worth today. Nor is it as fully formed a creation as the later GTX, which we called a "gentleman's muscle car" that expertly combined luxury and performance. Probably, if you want this Belvedere, you don't care about any of that. You're here for the vibes and the output.

Which is dandy, because according to the listing, a former NASCAR engine builder both bored and stroked the engine using an Indy cylinder-head stroker kit to achieve the larger displacement. So they started with the right 426 block (even if it's not original to this car), then modified it. And you probably wouldn't want the original motor, since it was a pretty pedestrian 225-cubic-inch Slant Six. These were ubiquitous, if not special, oddly tilted engines that refused to die. Anyway, boring the 426 to 588 cubic inches is an historically honest process of chasing power and less weird than, say, adding a turbo.

If you study the 2020 Bring a Trailer listing and compare it to the present one, you can see that the current owner has tried to push the Belvedere in a slightly more historically accurate direction. For instance, they swapped American Racing Torq Thrust D wheels with BFGoodrich Radial T/A tires for body-color 15-inch steel wheels. The latter are shod with Firestone Deluxe Champion front tires and 255/70 piecrust rear slicks. (If they'd made a meaningful performance upgrade, it might have been to swap the manual front disc and rear drum brakes, but these remain.)

Actual A990 cars saw not only up to 425 horsepower, but significant efforts by the factory to reduce weight. Chyrsler cut fat from the body, using only thin-gauge steel, and the cabin had no rear seat, with only a pair of buckets up front (without headrests). This BaT Belvedere, paying proper homage, doesn't have a radio or a heater, as was the case for A990s.

If you're considering a purchase, know that the listing states that the odometer no longer works. Even though this six-decade-old Belvedere has supposedly logged 81,000 miles, that's probably incorrect. The listing also notes oil leaks, and you can see in the photos that the car was partially but not entirely repainted, with the roof and driver-side quarter panel getting stripping and retouching. Photos of that process look like the shop that did this work was thorough, but ideally you'd see the entire car get that treatment. This isn't the car's original hue, either; it was born wearing dark turquoise metallic paint with a tan-painted cabin.

The current owner made some mechanical upgrades worth mentioning, too, replacing the fuel pump, switching to a factory-style fuel tank behind the rear axle, and moving the battery to the trunk. Does any of that matter if you lust after this monster? Probably not. Just note that original A990s have sold for as high as $200,000, which is extraordinary when you consider the inflation-adjusted sticker price of $4,500 should amount to maybe $50,000. But this isn't an actual A990. Which is probably a good thing, since you can think of it as a car. Not an investment. And burn rubber, as nature, and Plymouth, intended.

#5457. Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

The findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

"What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," said lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention."

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults showed particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

The consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood."

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is important because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

The findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

"Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," said Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support."

The study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an important role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Said Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked."

#5455. Happy Thanksgiving From Guangzhou, Visiting XPENG

While many in the US are celebrating Thanksgiving, I am seeing some of the most advanced technology and most impressive EVs in the world. XPENG offered to bring me to see AI day and Auto Guangzhou. I am thankful for the opportunity. Expect to hear more in depth in the days to come.

After renewing my Chinese driving permit, I was able to drive the sporty P7 again and use NGP with VLA 2.0 to and from XPENG’s increasingly automated and clean factory. That is simply a great car to drive. Acceleration is smooth and powerful. Despite the motor torque, the chassis can more than handle it. It feels both connected and comfortable in a balance that can be hard to find in many cars. And it looks great, especially in the dark green of the test car. I wish I had time to take it to some twisty backroads. However, the intelligent driving system makes dense urban traffic far more tolerable. At the times when you don’t want to drive, NGP drives the car flawlessly. Over the past year I have seen the system evolve, and it now offers even greater perception, smoothness, and efficiency. It is something you must experience to fully appreciate.

I also had the opportunity to ride in the YoYo Robotaxi with my friend Dan Caesar. Compared to some other robotaxi systems, it is a definite step up in comfort. More like limo service than a traditional taxi. The driving is extremely smooth, as is the ride, even in the congested and unpredictable roads in China. It drives much better than a typical human or some of the competitors I sampled. With the seat reclined, massage on and excellent entertainment system playing music or movies, I didn’t want to leave. I could have used another lap. I’ll have more details soon.

The following day, I attended XPENG AI Day. Over the course of the multi-hour event and Q&A, the amount of technological progress I was exposed to was expansive. Not only did I get to hear in depth about all the technological developments at XPENG, but I also was able to ask the IRON humanoid robot a question. With roughly half of the company dedicated to R&D, the speed of progress is impressive.

During the presentation, I heard about major developments in intelligent driving, including innovations that increase efficiency and range. I also heard about milestones being accomplished in flying cars, which took off in a demonstration the next day. However, the humanoid robot walking in to demonstrate the progress ahead of mass production clearly attracted the most attention.

I would like to think that I have a better understanding of these topics than many people, given the experience I have had so far. But the new helping of ideas and concepts was too much for me to process. My brain feels completely stuffed. Like that extra helping of Thanksgiving dinner, it will take a little bit for me to digest everything I have seen. Keep an eye out for more in-depth reports.

However, information was not the only thing I was gorging myself on. The food is exceptionally good in Guangzhou. While I have had great food at restaurants here, my favorite food is at the XPENG headquarters cafeteria at Mom’s Kitchen. This program lets the parents of employees set up shop to sell food at the cafeteria. As many employees come from different parts of the country, the program gives  them a taste of home. I am not sure what the dishes that I was eating were called, but there is something simply better about a home cooked meal. It may not look fancy, but the flavors were amazing. In addition, the hotel had turkey available for dinner, so I didn’t miss out on food.

I also was able to explore some Fall foliage. However, the leaves do not change color here in Guangzhou. Flowers are in bloom year-round, giving it the nickname “Flower City.” As I had done the standard headquarters tour before, I was able to split off with Tanya of XPENG to explore the grounds. Next to the headquarters building is a park with running trails, a pond and a river running through it, including a small waterfall. Throughout the year, there are events in the park, including concerts.

What is particularly impressive in the park is that much of this was bare dirt from the construction of XPENG’s headquarters when I visited in last November. Over the past year, grass, plants and trees were planted. The river was cleaned up to be clean and clear, with people fishing in its waters. Something that I would not imagine doing in most urban rivers. The planting is still in progress, but the environmental restoration is already impressive. And it is a reminder of how important it is to balance industry with nature.

On days that are not too hot, employees will often take their lunches outside or even take out mats to take a nap on the lawn. As the trees grow in further, the shade will increase and improve the comfort further. The park is also open to the public, and you can often see children playing. I heard the most difficult part is that people wish they had more time to enjoy the park. But XPENG has been remarkably busy.

Tomorrow, is Black Friday. A day dedicated to buying stuff. However, I will be at Auto Guangzhou looking at a wide range of exciting vehicles that I can’t buy in the United States. Better cars that are better because they are EVs. Cutting edge technology, premium amenities, and impressive build quality at affordable prices. Vehicles that give you new perspective on what’s possible.

I was able to see clear progress in the industry from the show last November to the Beijing show in April. Although XPENG is launching their models globally, many other brands launch in their home market first. Seeing the speed, progress and competition is invigorating having come from a market that often feels like it is stalling, but it can also be a bit overwhelming. I feel lucky to have the opportunity to see it firsthand and hope I can give people a glimpse of what’s happening.

Overall, I feel thankful for the opportunities to see and experience the some of the most advanced clean technology in the world over the past year with CleanTechnica. I am especially thankful to XPENG for being so open about their technology and the underlying thinking. It has been enlightening to see how the progress is being made in China and how that progress is being brought to Europe. I thank the PR teams for taking such good care of me and answering my questions. I am also thankful to Jackery for showing me innovations in energy storage and solar that create solutions for customer needs in both the US and Europe. And I am also thankful for BMW showing me something to be hopeful about regarding EVs and manufacturing in the US.

I am also thankful for all the great people I have met. From technology leaders to media legends, I have consistently been impressed. I now often feel like I am visiting friends. Business travel can feel lonely, but I have rarely felt that this year.

I am thankful for our readers, who make this possible. I often feel like I am learning from their comments as much as they are learning from what I write.

And I am thankful for my wife for putting up with all my nerdy conversations and trips away from home. And I am thankful for my cats, who are always happy to see me. I’ll be home soon.

#5454. Ford Returns To The 24 Hours Of Le Mans With The 2027 GT41

Ford has a relatively short but lauded history with the 24 Hours of Le Mans. In the 1960s it won four years in a row with the GT40, and pop culture fell in love with the GT40 via the film "Le Mans," and then again decades later with "Ford V Ferrari." The Big Blue Oval returned to Le Mans in 2016 with the Ford GT, which came first in its class, and it continued to race through 2019. Now Ford is headed back to Le Mans in 2027 with its latest hypercar effort, the GT41. Its new FIA Endurance Championship racer was revealed Thanksgiving day on Ford Field, while a different heated rivalry plays out: the Detroit Lions vs. Chicago Bears game.

The LMDh car sports a livery featuring footballs, bald eagles, the Ford name, and the Spirit of Detroit, a statue that has sat downtown since 1958. The Ford family owns the Detroit Lions, as well as a controlling share in the auto manufacturer that bears their name. This is the kind of synergy newer oligarchs wish they could achieve.

Powering the new GT41 is a naturally aspirated 5.4-liter V8 that's based on the same Coyote engine any old Ford-head can get in Mustangs and F-150s. The Coyote in the GT41 has been, of course, lovingly and painstakingly modified and rebuilt over and over again to drill down to peak Ford performance. The company then worked hard to destroy these delicately crafted pieces of machinery to ensure longevity during 24 hours of continuous driving. Ford is doing all of the development and testing in-house to make sure this new racer is the manufacturer's most ambitious program yet, born out of lessons learned during F1 Red Bull racing development.

It was 60 years ago when Ford swept the race in 1966, taking positions 1, 2 and 3. The manufacturer's program ended in 1967, but the GT40 went on to three more consecutive races, just with other operators, until 1969. That car was called GT40 because it stood 40 inches from the ground to the air intake; the new GT41 has grown by a single inch.

There is a direct line from the sport of kings to the global dominance of the car, and Ford had its hand in both. It was developing and racing his own automobiles 125 years ago that got Henry Ford interested in cars in the first place. Racing awards turned into seed money for manufacturing, and the rest is history.

The Ford GT41 already has a full suite of drivers, so sorry if you were planning on putting your name into the hat. Taking the wheel will be Logan Sargeant, Tom Blomqvist, Matt Campbell, Sebastian Priaulx, Mike Rockenfeller and Nick Yelloly, plus Tom Dillmann, who was recently announced as reserve driver. Running a car for 24 hours is a lot to ask of a single driver, after all. To really cement things, Ford has a new ad campaign using Carroll Shelby's motto "Go Like Hell," with voiceover work from "Ford V Ferrari' actor Matt Damon, who portrayed Shelby in the film.

This time it's not just Ferrari that Ford is looking to beat, though Ferrari did win in 2023, 2024 and 2025, so Ford should definitely be looking over its shoulder. 2027 is proving to be a crowed year for the WEC, with 12 different factory prototypes going head-to-head at Le Mans, including this year's new kid on the block, Genesis. Next year's 24 Hours of Le Mans will be a race worth remembering, no matter who comes out on top.

#5453. New Obesity Definition Flags More Adults at Dementia Risk

— Dementia risk shifts as obesity definition expands

A new definition of obesity identified more adults with an increased risk of dementia compared with defining obesity by body mass index (BMI) alone, pooled data from two cohorts showed.

Using the European Association for the Study of Obesity (EASO) definition, more than 80% of adults classified as overweight were reclassified as having obesity, according to Rui Zhou, PhD, of Guangdong Pharmaceutical University in Guangzhou, China, and co-authors.

Compared with people of normal weight without comorbidities, those with EASO-defined obesity had a significantly higher risk of dementia (pooled HR 1.93, 95% CI 1.50-2.48), Zhou and colleagues reported in Neurology.

Those with EASO-defined overweight, on the other hand, had a lower risk of dementia than those with normal weight (pooled HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.45-0.81).

The EASO framework incorporates BMI, body fat distribution (waist-to-height ratio), and medical, functional, or psychological comorbidities.

"These findings underscore the inadequacy of using BMI alone to define obesity," Zhou said in a statement. "The results support the integration of body fat distribution and other health conditions into classifying obesity."

Obesity is linked with dementia, with midlife obesity having an especially high risk. Evidence from both animal and human studies suggests that obesity negatively affects the brain through multiple mechanisms, including hypothalamic dysregulation and metabolic, inflammatory, and vascular disruptions that target the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.

The BMI definition of obesity has drawn criticism in recent years, leading to alternative frameworks from groups like EASO and the Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology global commission.

The implications of the new obesity definitions for dementia risk have been unclear, Zhou and co-authors noted. To help clarify this, they compared the prevalence of obesity under the EASO framework versus traditional BMI criteria and examined how obesity was associated with incident dementia and all-cause mortality.

The study used data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA; 6,542 people) and the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS; 12,402 people).

The researchers defined dementia using algorithmic criteria or self-reported physician diagnoses, and determined all-cause mortality from death registries, medical records, or interviews with relatives. They included 17,617 participants in the dementia analysis and 18,197 in the mortality analysis.

The mean baseline age in the ELSA group was 65.9 years and 54.3% were women. In CHARLS, the mean baseline age was 58.2 and 53.2% were women. The median follow-up was 11.5 years in ELSA and 8.2 years in CHARLS.

Under the EASO framework, 85.8% of ELSA participants and 80.2% of CHARLS participants who were previously classified as overweight by BMI shifted to the obesity category.

Overall, 37.7% of ELSA participants and 24.9% of CHARLS participants had obesity using the EASO definition. The most common comorbidities in the newly defined obesity group were high blood pressure (42.6%) and diabetes (35.1%).

Compared with people with normal weight and no comorbidities, people with EASO-defined obesity had higher dementia risk in both cohorts. They had higher mortality risk only in the CHARLS cohort, but the pooled mortality estimate was significant (pooled HR 1.30, 95% CI 1.01-1.68).

EASO-defined overweight was associated with lower dementia risk in both cohorts and with lower mortality (pooled HR 0.32, 95% CI 0.13-0.81).

The so-called "obesity paradox" seen in earlier studies may stem from failures to account for obesity-related comorbidities or to exclude unhealthy individuals from comparison groups, the researchers suggested.

When normal weight without morbidity was the reference in this study, both EASO-defined and BMI-defined obesity were consistently associated with increased dementia risk, they noted. "However, when all normal weight individuals (including those with comorbidities) were used as the reference, these harmful associations were masked," Zhou and colleagues pointed out.

Obesity was measured only at baseline, and changes over time were not captured, the researchers acknowledged. Despite adjusting for multiple variables, residual confounding cannot be excluded.

#5452. Jessica Alba Ordered To Pay Cash Warren $577K—Inside Her Recent Beverly Hills Real Estate Moves

Jessica Alba’s divorce from Cash Warren is back in the headlines after a new court order awarded Warren $577,481 from Alba’s retirement benefits.

The ruling comes after the former couple sold their longtime Beverly Hills–area home and Alba later purchased another property in the area.

The retirement award comes from Alba’s account in the HonorBar Inc. Profit Sharing Plan, according to court documents reported by TMZ.

Any money left in the account after Warren receives his share is to go to Alba. The documents also allow Warren to take the award as a lump sum or move it into an individual retirement account or another retirement plan.

The court order also addresses account records: If Warren requests statements in writing within the next year, Alba must provide them within 10 days.

According to the outlet, transferring the money into a retirement account could avoid a 20% tax withholding.

The ruling is the latest financial development following the couple’s divorce, which was finalized in February 2026.

It was previously reported that Alba was ordered to pay Warren $3 million to balance the division of their assets.

Their settlement also divided interests in several companies, shares in The Honest Company, and residuals from projects made during their marriage.

Meanwhile, Alba and Warren have already put their real estate ties behind them.

Their former Beverly Hills–area home was sold in 2025. Alba and Warren purchased the seven-bedroom estate for $9.9 million in 2017, then put it on the market in April 2025 for $18.99 million. It was sold for $18.2 million, with the closing recorded on June 27, 2025.

The property sat on about 1.86 acres and included 8.5 bathrooms, a guesthouse, a home theater, and extensive grounds.

Alba and Warren undertook an 18-month renovation after buying it, with Alba involved in decisions about the home’s design.

After the sale, Alba picked up a splashy Beverly Hills estate in September 2025 for $4.75 million.

The two transactions mark a change in Alba’s recent housing history: the end of her and Warren’s ownership of a sprawling family estate, followed by her purchase of another Beverly Hills property.

Alba and Warren announced their separation in December 2024 after 16 years of marriage.

Alba filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences, and the sale of their longtime home followed the announcement.

#5450. Tiny magnets deep inside the brain could transform Parkinson’s treatment

An international research team has developed a new technique that uses magnetic fields and tiny particles to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, potentially opening the door to a less invasive treatment for Parkinson's disease. In experiments involving mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms, the approach significantly improved movement problems without requiring permanently implanted electrodes.

The technique involves injecting specially designed magnetic nanoplatelets into a targeted area of the brain. When exposed to an external magnetic field, these particles generate tiny forces that activate nearby nerve cells. Unlike conventional brain stimulation treatments, which rely on surgically implanted electrodes, the new approach uses magnetic forces to influence brain activity. The findings, published in Advanced Science, come from researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU), RWTH Aachen, and the Universities of Maastricht (the Netherlands) and Leuven (Belgium).

Why Parkinson's Treatment Often Requires Brain Implants

Parkinson's disease develops as brain cells responsible for producing dopamine gradually break down. Dopamine is a chemical messenger that plays a vital role in controlling movement. As its levels decline, communication within the brain's movement circuits becomes disrupted, contributing to tremors and other motor difficulties.

For some patients, deep brain stimulation can help control these symptoms. This treatment uses a device known as a brain pacemaker, which is implanted beneath the collarbone and connected to electrodes placed deep inside the brain. The electrodes deliver electrical stimulation to a region called the subthalamic nucleus (STN for short), helping to modify abnormal activity in the brain circuits responsible for movement.

Although this treatment can provide substantial relief, it requires a complex surgical procedure and does not work for everyone.

"The procedure is relatively complex, however, and not always successful," explains Prof. Dr. Danijela Gregurec from the Department of Chemistry and Pharmacy at FAU. "This puts many Parkinson's patients off, and not all patients are suitable candidates for one of these pacemakers."

The researchers believe magnetic stimulation could eventually provide another option, allowing doctors to influence the same deep brain structures without leaving electrodes permanently implanted.

How Tiny Magnetic Particles Stimulate Brain Cells

The new technology takes advantage of the ability of certain nerve cells to detect physical pressure and mechanical forces.

"We use magnetic nanoparticles that we implant in the brain," Gregurec explains. "They have a special shape and a magnetic structure. They were developed in order to transform magnetic fields into tiny mechanical forces."

Rather than sending electrical pulses directly into the brain, the technique uses these particles to produce extremely small physical movements when a magnetic field is applied.

"The traditional method establishes an electrical connection to the brain," she says. "In contrast, we use the neurons' natural mechanosensors to influence regions deep within the brain."

The process works by gently changing the shape of nearby nerve cell membranes. Imagine pressing a finger against an inflated balloon and creating a small indentation in its surface. The magnetic particles produce a similar effect on a microscopic scale.

This slight deformation opens specialized channels in the cell membrane that respond to mechanical pressure. Once opened, these channels allow electrically charged particles called ions to enter the nerve cells, changing their electrical activity and providing a way to stimulate the targeted brain circuits.

Magnetic Brain Stimulation Improves Movement in Mice

To investigate whether the technology could relieve Parkinson's symptoms, the international research team conducted experiments using mice with damage to the same types of dopamine-producing nerve cells affected by the disease in humans. This damage caused movement difficulties resembling those seen in Parkinson's patients.

"Together with our partners from Maastricht, we injected magnetic nanoparticles developed here at FAU into the animals' subthalamic nucleus," Gregurec explains. "That is the very region in the brain that is also an important target for conventional deep brain stimulation in Parkinson's disease."

The researchers used precise stereotactic injection techniques to deliver the particles to the intended location. These methods rely on carefully calculated three-dimensional coordinates to guide instruments into specific brain structures. Accurate placement was particularly important because the treatment needed to affect the correct neural circuits involved in movement.

After the particles were positioned, the researchers applied an external magnetic field. The results were encouraging: the mice showed significant improvements in their movement deficits.

"The effect is roughly equivalent to what we would have expected after implanting a brain pacemaker," says Gregurec.

The findings suggest that magnetic nanoparticles could provide a different way to achieve some of the benefits of conventional deep brain stimulation, without the need for permanently implanted electrodes.

Could Future Parkinson's Treatments Use Magnetic Headbands?

Another encouraging finding involved how the brain responded to the implanted particles over time. The magnetic nanoparticles remained in place throughout an observation period lasting several months, and the researchers found no signs of inflammation. This suggests that the particles were well tolerated during the experiments.

However, delivering the particles still required an injection directly into the brain. Gregurec and her colleagues are now investigating ways to make the procedure even less invasive.

One possibility is to develop particles that could be injected into the bloodstream and then travel into the brain by crossing the blood-brain barrier. This protective boundary normally prevents many substances circulating in the blood from entering brain tissue. Finding a way to deliver the particles across it could eliminate the need for direct brain injections.

The researchers are also exploring compact wearable devices capable of generating the magnetic fields needed for stimulation. One possibility is a headband that patients could put on themselves, potentially making treatment more convenient and adjustable.

These ideas remain at an early stage, and the researchers expect that several more years of development will be needed before the technology could be considered for clinical use.

"Nevertheless, we are convinced that the new method has enormous potential," Gregurec states. "It is not only considerably simpler and cheaper than a conventional brain pacemaker, it is probably also more flexible. Adjusting the parameters of the magnetic field would allow us to control the nanoparticles more accurately."

Beyond its potential medical applications, the technology could also become a valuable scientific tool. By allowing researchers to stimulate nerve cells through carefully controlled mechanical forces, it offers a new way to explore how physical changes at the cellular level influence brain activity.

Although the treatment has so far been demonstrated only in animals, its ability to improve movement without permanently implanted electrodes represents a promising step toward new approaches to Parkinson's disease and brain stimulation.

#5449. Inside Elizabeth Holmes’ Secret Oceanfront Rental Seen in ‘You Can See Everything’ Documentary a Month Before She’s Sent to Prison

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” takes place in the Theranos founder’s former Del Mar, CA, rental—and the property’s location in an exclusive, gated community could be just part of the reason the film’s unexpected release was such a smash.

The project—which is now available to stream on demand and was directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim—was kept secret for the four years it was in production, leaving viewers in awe after the documentary’s surprise Sept. 6 premiere at Telluride Film Festival.

Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, invited the film crew—which Oppenheim told Variety was intentionally kept intimate to keep the project a secret—to reside in the guesthouse of the home for the 34 days before she reported to Federal Prison Camp in Bryan, TX, on May 30, 2023.

“Keeping it under wraps was very important because we never wanted to get in front of what we were capturing,” the director shared.

The crew would typically shoot for 16-hour days, with Fielder telling Variety that cameras were strategically positioned to “cover the whole house” so nothing would be missed.

The four-bedroom, four-bathroom beachfront property is located in an ultraprivate community less than a half-hour from San Diego. Called Sandy Lane, it features just about a dozen residences.

“This is basically a hidden community. It’s a guard-gated community, which is so rare on a beach, which is why you have a lot of high-profile individuals up and down this strip,” celebrity real estate agent Josh Altman explained in a home tour of another property on the community’s sole street.

Given the home's private location—and considering California’s anti-paparazzi legislation protecting private property from capture—it’s plain to see why Holmes and Evans opted to rent the 2,200-square-foot dwelling in the time leading up to her imprisonment.

The New York Times also previously reported that the couple and their two children moved to the area to be nearer to Evans’ family. His parents, William L. Evans and Susan Evans, are the hotel magnates behind Evans Hotels, a San Diego–based hospitality company.

Although the property is currently off-market, a previous listing indicates the single-story home was built in 1948 and includes direct access to the private beach.

As seen in the film, the abode features tall ceilings with exposed-beams and sizable windows connecting the home to the serene surrounding landscape. Midcentury modern design is present throughout the home, which is paneled in honey-hued wood.

While Realtor.com® estimates the property’s current market value to be about $5.8 million, it’s unclear just how much Holmes and Evans shelled out to reside there temporarily.
