#5416. How artificial intelligence is offering new hope for stroke patients in the Last Frontier

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Katie covers the impact of health technology on patients, clinicians, and businesses. Her stories explore the price tag of clinical AI, digital health at the FDA, and the boom in direct-to-consumer telehealth. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at palmer.01.

It was just after lunchtime when the doctor’s phone started to vibrate and chime. On this summer Wednesday, a neurointerventionalist in Anchorage got the alert: Three hundred miles away, at a hospital deep in Alaska’s interior, a clot in a major artery was blocking the flow of blood to a patient’s brain. He needed it out — and he’d have to come to the state’s biggest city to get it done.

Time is never on a stroke patient’s side. Every minute without blood flow, 2 million brain cells die. And in Alaska — a state more than double the size of Texas, most of it inaccessible by road — it can take several hours to arrange a plane, airlift a patient to Ted Stevens airport in Anchorage, and deliver them by ambulance to one of the five neurointerventionalists in the entire state who can extract clots.

In his mid-60s, the patient on the doctor’s phone had arrived at a nearby emergency room after a morning fall, suddenly weak on his left side. Like most patients with stroke symptoms, he got a head CT, which helps diagnose a stroke, whether it’s caused by a clot or a brain bleed, and determine whether that clot can be broken up with drugs or needs to be extracted. Normally, once the scan is complete, it could take 45 precious minutes just to send those thousands of two-dimensional brain snapshots to Anchorage for review — 90 million brain cells before a doctor could accept his transfer.

But this summer day, the patient had a new type of technology on his team. Stroke is the fourth-leading cause of death in the United States, the majority caused by occlusions that block blood flow to the brain, and survival rates are significantly worse for rural patients. In recent years, states have built up stroke networks, including telestroke care and automated artificial intelligence analysis, to try to improve transfer times for patients without access to specialist neurological care. One of the latest additions was in Alaska — where, starting in 2023, a small network of hospitals had agreed to use the same AI software to triage stroke patients and get them to the right care, faster.

Nearly instantly, the tool, from RapidAI, analyzed his CT scan for signs of a large vessel occlusion, or LVO, a type of blockage that often needs to be mechanically sucked out or retrieved with a stent. Through an app used by other hospitals with the technology, the results went out to his local team of doctors and the faraway network of neurointerventionalists — one of whom was on call at Providence Alaska Medical Center in Anchorage.

The app alerted the doctor with the results just seconds after the scan was complete: suspected LVO. Less than a half hour after the patient arrived at his local ER, the team had called Providence for a transfer — two minutes before their on-call radiologist even delivered their official CT report.

Four hours and 23 minutes later, the clot was out. Without the AI assist, it would have taken at least an extra hour.

In 2026, it’s not rare for a hospital to use AI to triage stroke patients. Eight years ago, clinical trials showed that automated image analysis could extend the clot removal window for stroke patients as late as 24 hours after they were last well — before this, the window was just six hours. At the same time, the Food and Drug Administration approved the first AI to detect large vessel occlusions.

Those “were the wonder years,” said Stanford neurologist Greg Albers, co-founder of RapidAI. “Stroke centers scrambled to access the software.” Developers started to bundle different stroke algorithms in one package, driven by vendors like Viz.ai, Aidoc, and Brainomix, along with RapidAI.

As with most new medical technology, though, that adoption has been uneven. At the forefront of the deployment were large metropolitan hospitals, including those categorized as comprehensive stroke centers.

“Maybe it’s because they had more advanced workflows in place. Maybe it’s because they had the funding to acquire this AI software,” said Casey Pelzl, a researcher at the Harvey L. Neiman Health Policy Institution who studied some of the technology’s early adoption. “But what we know about stroke is that a lot of patients seek initial treatment at noncomprehensive stroke care centers, and these are the places that could potentially benefit from it the most.”

That’s the promise that a small group of stroke coordinators and neurointerventionalists in Alaska saw in 2023, when they established a volunteer nonprofit called the Alaska Stroke Coalition in a bid to improve stroke outcomes in a state that throws up obstacles at every turn.

“The distances that we have to cross are enormous. The weather that we have to face is awful. Resource availability is so low,” said Kelly Isaacs, Providence’s stroke program manager. Sometimes Alaskans arrive at their village clinics by snow machine or dogsled. The state doesn’t have consistent reporting of stroke outcomes. And in the summer months, when cruise ships wind up the coast, a seaside hub’s population can swell nearly tenfold, often enriched with older passengers. Jaded hospital workers sometimes call them the “stroke boats.”

Against those unfavorable odds, one thing that could improve patients’ chances of survival after a stroke is getting them to the right care as fast as possible. “‘Time is brain’ is still very much the case, and the more quickly you can start a treatment — whether it’s the drug to break up the clot or if it’s a big clot, to transport them where they can get the clot taken out — that’s going to make a big difference for people,” said UC Health neurologist and stroke researcher Joseph Broderick.

By 2023, a few hospitals in the state, mostly in Anchorage, had started using RapidAI’s software, but barely any regional hospitals in the state’s interior and on its far-flung coasts did. Even for those hospitals that had the tech, “the challenge was we existed in all these different systems, but we weren’t coordinated,” said David Stoffel, RapidAI’s chief business officer. Each hospital had its own software license and didn’t share information within the app, making it difficult to coordinate decision-making for patients who might have needed a transfer.

So the newly formed Alaska Stroke Coalition, whose founders included Isaacs, tried to build a solution. Lucy He, a neurointerventionalist in Alaska, found funding from a family foundation to buy RapidAI for six additional hospitals spread across the state, at a cost of about $450,000. The resulting network spread from Alaska’s very northernmost tip in Utqiagvik, all the way south to the state’s capital of Juneau, which can only be accessed by air or water. When the tech threw up an alert about possible LVO in a patient, the message wouldn’t just circulate within that hospital team — it would go out wide, to the neurointerventionalists in Anchorage who might be able to help.

In return for the coalition paying for the AI tool, the health systems agreed to report their performance over the next three years, to see if the technology could really make a difference.

Day to day, the stroke coordinators and doctors accepting patients from across the state saw the technology changing their decision-making. It wasn’t always about quickly transferring patients for treatment — sometimes it was about making the hard calls to stay put.

Kevin Myrick, one of the coalition’s founders and Providence’s stroke program coordinator, pointed to a patient transferred to Providence this summer: a man in his 80s with a large vessel occlusion and severe symptoms. Patients like him are usually paralyzed on one side and lose speech. When strokes are this bad, it is far from given that a patient will regain function after treatment: Dead brain tissue is dead, forever. And restoring blood flow to dead tissue can do more harm than good, reintroducing toxic metabolic byproducts into circulation and causing swelling and bleeding.

“We did not put this [technology] in to transfer every patient to Anchorage,” said Myrick. If a patient doesn’t have enough chance for recovery, it can be preferable to keep them closer to home — to save them expense, keep them near their support network, and avoid using limited EMS staff time and planes.

In these cases, it’s a head CT with a contrast agent showing detailed blood flow in the brain that can help doctors tell what intervention is worthwhile. In the Rapid app, that image looks like a series of brain slices colored in neon-bright, Lisa Frank shades of green and pink. Pink tissue is gone. Green is brain that has the potential to be salvaged if blood flow is restored in time. “In Alaska, where you’ve got those big distances, having that imaging is going to be really important about deciding who to send and why to send,” said Broderick, of UC Health.

For the patient in his 80s, the CT perfusion images that came through the app showed far more green tissue than pink, their volumes neatly tabulated in milliliters by the software. “This patient was definitely a go,” said Myrick. He traveled 750 miles — about the distance from New York City to Chicago — and within a few minutes of arrival was shuttled into Providence’s catheterization lab, its team ready and waiting.

A CT scan after the clot removal shows his brain in profile. Blood fills the main arteries and tangled branches that supply oxygen throughout the entire brain; in his first CT, nearly half of that field was blank, its roadways cut off by the clot. Still weak and with impaired speech after the mechanical thrombectomy, he has a long way to go, said Isaacs. But “when he got sent home, he’s got a much better chance of recovery than he would have otherwise.”

The technology isn’t perfect. Like most radiology algorithms, there are false positives — scans that the app will say show a large vessel occlusion that actually don’t. It takes a good image to work well, said Broderick: “Sometimes, when you look at the pictures, if the person moves or the study wasn’t done right, the data is not good.” That means a doctor still reviews every output, and that official read is what drives the call to transfer or not. And for the biggest returns, it requires a hospital to actually perform CT perfusion imaging, which hasn’t been uniformly adopted in hospitals that don’t remove clots themselves.

But despite the limitations, the hospitals that have received the technology through the coalition’s grant are enthusiastic about connecting more of Alaska with the same alert system. “In rural Alaska, at all these tribal health organization hospitals, I think that that really can change the narrative here,” said Dylan Latif, stroke coordinator at Alaska Native Medical Center, one of the program’s grantees, at a meeting of the coalition in early October.

“If we do this with a bunch of different hospitals, then we create, you know, the Skynet of stroke in Alaska,” said He, the neurointerventionalist, at the same meeting.

The stroke coalition hasn’t yet published research about how the technology has impacted stroke care for Alaskans. But early data point to a recent increase in the number of thrombectomies delivered in Alaska, which could be driven in part by the program. And once patients arrived in Anchorage, hospitals with cath labs saw about a 30% improvement in the time it takes to start threading a device in to retrieve a clot.

“Logistically, every cath lab in America during normal business hours is booked 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. all day, every day,” Isaacs explained. With coordinated alerts from referring hospitals, it can be easier to prepare for stroke patients’ arrival. “We’ve got our little flight tracker up, and we’re like, OK, they’re 30 minutes out,” she said.

As is so often the case with AI deployed in health care, it will be longer before Alaska can show whether the new technology is changing the outcomes that matter the most: rates of long-term disability and death from strokes. It’s especially challenging in Alaska, where detailed data has been scarce; more complete stroke intervention and outcome recording began at the same time the coalition expanded the use of AI.

“Can I give you statistically significant information that RapidAI has made a big difference in the state of Alaska?” said Isaacs. “I can’t, really.”

For now, some doctors who care for stroke patients in Alaska are optimistic. “Being able to take these people who are from way the heck out of the middle of nowhere, they got 45 minutes to the local scanner, and now they are deemed eligible for an intervention — it has saved countless numbers of patients,” said Ryan Wilson, a neurologist at Alaska Native Medical Center, to his colleagues during the October meeting. “They’re gaining their brain back.”

As the members of the Alaska Stroke Coalition face down the end of their three-year grant period, that enthusiasm is translating into action: Each one of the six hospitals that got free access to RapidAI has said it wants to keep and pay for it. And there’s hope for even more significant changes to the landscape of stroke care in the state.

“Coincidentally, three things happened that help us further that mission,” said Isaacs.

The first happened this February, when the American Heart Association and the American Stroke Association released new stroke guidelines. The previous guidelines suggested narrow windows in which a patient could be treated with clot-busting drugs: They had 4 1/2 hours to get the medication. But in the updated guidelines, depending on how much salvageable tissue a patient appears to have in one of those pink-and-green CT perfusion images, they can still receive the drugs nine, even 24 hours after symptoms started.

That could dramatically increase the number of treatable stroke patients in Alaska — especially those who can be treated in place by clot-busting drugs. With RapidAI in more hospitals, Isaacs hopes that perfusion imaging will become more common, helping to make those calls about whether a patient falls in those extended windows. “Stroke used to be way more depressing to take care of, because our treatment options were very limited,” she said. “The windows were very short, and now with increased technology and increased time in our guidelines, it’s not quite as sad as it used to be, honestly.”

The second boost came in June, when Alaska enacted a law that will help establish statewide standards for strokes and heart attacks, like it already had in place for trauma. “We always sort of looked over at what trauma had, and we were like, ‘Isn’t that great? They’ve got designations, they get site visits, they’ve got data collection. We need these things,’” said Isaacs, who, along with several other coalition members, voiced support for the bill.

And in October, the final piece of the puzzle fell into place: The coalition got word that the work it’s been doing is primed to expand. “They got proof of concept that they can achieve this equity of care in Alaska for stroke,” said RapidAI’s Stoffel, and leveraged it in an application to the five-year, $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program.

In the first year of funding, the Alaska Stroke Coalition received $3.2 million of the state’s funding to start building a statewide AI imaging network.

With grant-funded hospitals and independent purchases combined, Alaska will soon have 21 acute care hospitals and two CT scan-enabled clinics with RapidAI’s stroke system in place. “This is phenomenal for Alaska,” said RapidAI’s Albers. “There are financial issues for some of these smaller hospitals, and I think they’re even more significant in Alaska than elsewhere.”

The group hopes to receive funding for at least two more years — first, to build support infrastructure that allows for rapid decisions to transfer or keep patients, and then track the financial impact of the technology on hospitals.

“As a girl who was born and raised in Alaska, this is the most Alaskan story that you can get,” Isaacs said to the room of her colleagues in the coalition’s October meeting. Earlier that day, she had gotten the email confirming the grant funding. “It’s like, ‘Oh, you don’t want to do it? Fine, we’ll go do it ourselves.’ And here we are.”

#5415. ‘The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey’ Puts Family’s Former Boulder, CO, Residence in the Spotlight Once Again

Nearly 30 years after 6-year-old JonBenét Ramsey was found dead in her family’s home in Boulder, CO, the tragic case is regaining attention with the release of a new Netflix limited series.

“The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” tells the story of the cold case through a lens that seeks not to solve the mystery, but to tell the story of those who were involved—particularly as the 1996 murder occurred in a decade marked by high-profile crime.

The 1990s "ended with Columbine and started with the Menendez brothers, the Susan Smith murder, the OJ trial,” showrunner Richard LaGravenese said in a statement. “I was fascinated by the challenge of doing something that was a murder mystery without an ending, without being solved.”

To portray the effects of the media coverage that surrounded the case, the limited series will focus on Patsy and John Ramsey (played by Melissa McCarthy and Clive Owen) as well as a group of local and federal investigators (brought to life by Garrett Hedlund, Will Patton, Shea Whigham, and Alison Pill).

“They all had different points of view for all different reasons,” LaGravenese said. “It was an incredible story to tell from all these perspectives.”

The Ramsey family’s former home was at the center of the case, and although a handful of interior and exterior shots in the series’ trailer strikingly resemble the recognizable Tudor, it has been reported that “The Murder of JonBenét Ramsey” was filmed in Calgary, Alberta.

And while a few of the memorable details of the home—such as the black-and-white checkerboard tile floor in the kitchen—also make an appearance in the trailer, much of the home has been updated in recent years. Listing photos from 2024 show that the kitchen was entirely renovated.

The Ramseys purchased the home for $500,000 in 1991, and moved to Atlanta in 1997 following JonBenét’s death. They sold the home for $650,000 in 1998, with profits from the sale pledged to the JonBenét Ramsey Children’s Foundation.

The 7,240-square-foot abode changed hands again, for $1.05 million in 2004. Numerous attempts to sell the home since then have come to naught. In 2008, it was listed for $2.68 million; the price was later reduced to $2.29 million in 2009, $2.3 million in 2011, and $2 million in 2014.

Nine years would pass before the home was listed again, asking $6.95 million in March 2023. After a series of price adjustments, the property was taken off the market in February 2025.

JonBenét was found dead in the wine cellar in the basement of the home in the early hours of Dec. 26, 1996. Hours before her body was discovered, the family uncovered a ransom note in the home, which asked $118,000 for the return of their daughter.

Police determined she had been murdered in the late hours of the night on Christmas, and a later autopsy ruled the cause of death as strangulation.

In the following months, police investigated a number of suspects, including Patsy, John, and their son, Burke Ramsey—who were not cleared until July 2008, two years after Patsy died of ovarian cancer.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5414. Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF

Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The number of regions where patients have limited choices for Affordable Care Act plans is on the rise, according to a new analysis.

The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation report found that for the 2027 plan year, there are more than 200 counties in which there is only one insurer available, and close to 1,000 where there are just two plans available for consumers to choose from.

This makes for an increase of 50% from the 2026 plan year, with more than a third of counties having limited options on the ACA's marketplaces for 2027.

Most states (39) will have at least one county where plan choices are limited for enrollees. For about half of these states, this is the norm and aligns with 2026, but for the rest, this marks a significant shift, the RWJF researchers wrote in the report.

"For the individual market as a whole, the decline in participation is sobering but not a fatal blow," per the report. "The presence of federal and some state subsidies provides an important backstop that will likely prevent a complete meltdown."

"Yet the prospect of a growing number of counties with little insurer participation is grim, and likely will not bode well for premium increases, morbidity or enrollment going forward," according to the report.

The foundation cites a recent analysis from Wakely that found the individual market declined by 16% in the first six months of 2026. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits, cost pressures and growing administrative burdens are likely to contribute to worsening trends in this space.

For instance, ACA marketplace exits from Cigna, CareSource and Medica are having a significant impact in Iowa and Indiana for the coming plan year, the researchers found. In the latter case, most Indiana counties have two or fewer plan choices.

However, there are some bright spots, RWJF researchers wrote. There are certain insurers participating in the exchanges who have beefed up their footprints, and there is a smattering of new entrants. Oscar Health, for example, is planning the largest growth, entering a new state and adding new counties in some of the states it already serves.

Some insurers, like Centene and UnitedHealthcare, are making strategic exits in some markets while entering others, for a neutral impact on their footprints overall.

Insurers like Antidote Health and Peak Health are also entering new regions—even if on a limited basis in some cases—which can help staunch the bleeding.

Blue Cross Blue Shield plans also often play a key role in limited markets, as in close to 80% of counties with a single insurer, that payer is a Blues plan. In addition, in 12% of counties, the single insurer is Elevance Health, which operates plans as Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield.

"This suggests that were it not for the somewhat unique role of Blues plans as a backstop, the threat of a bare county might be higher," per the report. "Single-state Blues, in particular, are under social and political pressure to participate in much if not all of their state, and do not feel as free to exit unprofitable counties as are publicly traded insurers."

#5413. STAT+: AI can analyze X-rays and CT scans to draft radiology reports. Will it make care better, safer?

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Katie covers the impact of health technology on patients, clinicians, and businesses. Her stories explore the price tag of clinical AI, digital health at the FDA, and the boom in direct-to-consumer telehealth. Confidential tips can be sent on Signal at palmer.01.

For more than two decades, artificial intelligence has played a growing role in the practice of radiology. Today, nearly every radiologist uses AI tools, whether that’s to triage the images they interpret, dictate their reports, or detect findings in the dozens of X-rays and CTs they read every day.

But last year, radiology experts and developers at the annual meeting of the Radiological Society of North America began to foreground a new paradigm in AI. Business acquisitions and debates centered on technology, powered by vision-language models, that can do the core work of a radiologist: looking at an image, and drafting a report of the clinical findings within it.

“Last year’s RSNA was mainly focused on whether it’s actually possible that an AI model will write a draft for radiologists that would look like an actual radiology report, and that would be accurate enough to be even considered by a radiologist,” said Michael Braginsky, chief technology officer of Aidoc.

#5412. Catching up with the new CEO of UnitedHealthcare's Surest

Catching up with the new CEO of UnitedHealthcare's Surest" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Joe Clark is stepping into the CEO chair at UnitedHealthcare's Surest unit with an eye on affordability.

Clark was appointed to lead the division earlier this month, after serving as the chief financial officer for the insurer's employer and individual segment. In an interview with Fierce Healthcare, he said that the new role comes at "an exciting time" to be a part of a plan like Surest.

Under the model, Surest eliminates deductibles for a copayment-only approach, where members' costs are tied to the quality and value for their provider. Members connect to the Surest app or website to compare the cost between different providers.

"Affordability is a challenge every year, but especially right now, for employers," Clark said. "We've seen demand for Surest and other sort of alternative health plans just skyrocket over the last year. And being part of being able to deliver that and offer solutions to employers is incredibly exciting."

UnitedHealthcare first launched the unit in 2016 as Bind before rebranding as Surest in 2022 with an eye on growth. In a 2023 report, the company said that Surest members had 6% fewer emergency department visits and 13% fewer inpatient admissions compared to people enrolled in traditional commercial plans at the same company.

The plan also saw a 20% increase in visits to a physician and 9% increase in preventative physical exams compared to the members in traditional plans.

In a 2024 analysis, conducted by Aon, the company found that Surest enrollees generated $400 or more in cost claims savings per year. That study also identified improvements around spending and utilization across all age groups and accounting for several conditions.

Clark said that in a traditional health plan, only about 15% of people hit their deductible for the year, meaning they're ultimately not using their insurance during that time frame. Surest removes that problem by eliminating the deductible and puts the power in the consumers' hands to make choices for their own care.

He added that the Net Promoter Score for Surest is higher than its other commercial plan offerings. Consumers report satisfaction with the digital experience and the cost certainty that the plan presents, Clark said.

"It's very much like the Amazon shopping experience, but for healthcare, which hasn't happened before," Clark said.

Surest also aims to personalize the member experience by leaning on AI and other digital tools to present data on providers and costs that may be of use to the user, while leaving the ultimate decision in their hands.

"The consumer is in charge with their doctor in making those decisions," Clark said. "But we want to make sure that we are giving you, similar to what you would see with any shopping app, a personalized recommendation of what is a good fit."

Clark said that starting his career on the actuarial side of healthcare made plain how much of a challenge affordability can be, and that drew him to pursue his current path. Prior to UnitedHealthcare, he served as an associate partner at McKinsey and as an actuary at Cigna.

Through Surest, he believes he can help lead the charge toward a more modern healthcare system, he said.

As for the future of Surest, the first piece is continuing to make sure the team delivers on a personalized and simple-to-understand experience for consumers. The next level is building on that consumer-focused experience to add a provider layer, and work with them on the quality and value scores that are surfaced to members.

For example, a provider may consistently recommend a patient seek an MRI scan at a hospital rather than at a lower-cost lab. And Surest is gaining the "critical mass" of members where providers actively want to have these conversations, Clark said.

"I see that as sort of the next evolution beyond working with consumers and members: moving to providers as well," he said.

#5411. A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

A new review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

Treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an important part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

If, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The new review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

The findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is important given the average time people take them is much longer.

Importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

For someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

#5410. Opinion: Genomic testing is too fragmented. Instead, we should test once and evaluate often

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Hagman is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company.

Genomic testing can answer a variety of pressing health questions a person (and their clinician) might face throughout their lifespan.

Unfortunately, these valuable tests have become fragmented and iterative for most patients. A patient may receive a carrier screening test before or during pregnancy; a cancer predisposition test to screen for inherited cancer-predisposition variants like BRCA, the breast cancer gene; and a pharmacogenomic test before starting a medication. Each test is a new blood draw or buccal swab, a new wet lab workflow, a new spot on a genome sequencer, a new analysis, and new costs borne by patients and insurance companies.

With the precipitous decline in the cost of whole genome sequencing, it’s time to consolidate testing by sequencing genomes once and reevaluating them when needed.

As research has shown, patients face many challenges to accessing genomic testing including financial barriers, limited access to providers, geographic limitations, and clinician biases. Since the genome can enable diagnoses and care for so many health conditions, a more streamlined and uniform approach to genomic testing would likely benefit many patients. I call it “test once, evaluate often.”

A “test once, evaluate often” approach could start at any age. For some families, that might be at birth, as an optional add-on to the newborn screening their baby already gets. A single whole genome sequence could be stored, along with other medical records information, for future analysis. Any time a clinician orders a new genomic test, the lab would simply reevaluate the relevant genes and issue a report.

This approach would dramatically lower the cost and turnaround time needed to answer genomic questions by eliminating the sample handling and wet lab processing of patient samples, potentially improving access to genomic information for patients who would otherwise choose to forgo testing due to costs.

Such a paradigm would only apply to tests looking at germline DNA (the DNA we are born with). Clinical genomic tests seeking to understand the genetics of other biological characteristics, such as somatic DNA in a cancer tissue, circulating fetal DNA in a noninvasive prenatal test, or circulating tumor DNA in liquid biopsy panels would still be needed to look for genomic variants beyond germline DNA when patient circumstances dictate.

Newborn screening is one of public health’s great successes. For more than 60 years, nearly every U.S. baby has had a heel-prick blood test for dozens of serious, treatable conditions, catching thousands of babies each year who look perfectly healthy.

For many, early diagnosis is the difference between life and death. Infants with severe combined immunodeficiency who receive a transplant by 3.5 months survive 94% of the time. Babies destined for the most severe form of spinal muscular atrophy who receive gene therapy before symptoms emerge go on to sit independently and breathe without permanent ventilation. Any interruption to newborn screening would cost children their lives.

Genome sequencing builds on that foundation. In the BabySeq Project, 9.4% of newborns had an unexpected genetic risk for childhood-onset disease. In New York’s GUARDIAN study, 72% of families opted in and 3.7% of babies screened positive, including for treatable conditions that standard screening misses. Because sequencing alone misses some cases that biochemical tests catch, it should add to the heel prick, not replace it.

In childhood, reporting can stay focused on conditions where knowing early changes care; the rest of the genome can wait until there’s a question to answer. And as with any public health program, clear consent and transparent data use must be built in from the start.

The need for genomic information changes with patient circumstances and throughout their lifespan. This is why regular evaluation of the genome is needed in place of the piecemeal approach to ordering individual tests today.

Unfortunately, genomic science is not yet in a place where a single point of evaluation is practical. Evidence about emerging gene-disease relationships and new understandings of variants associated with hereditary cancer and other diseases continue to be adopted into clinical practice, meaning that an analysis conducted 20 years into the future would likely deliver more information than is currently possible.

The genomics community has honed a version of this practice, termed reanalysis, in the rare disease space. There, it is commonplace to reexamine a patient’s exome or genome based on emerging clinical evidence about gene-disease relationships.

Reevaluation is a bit different. Reanalysis is done for the same testing indication (i.e., finding the genetic cause of a rare disease) and reevaluation is studying the same genome for a new testing indication.

The National Human Genome Research Institute envisions a future where genomic data is systematically collected and used more regularly and efficiently for patient benefit. Getting there means moving clinical and laboratory medicine toward a system in which a genome sequenced once, whether at birth or later in life, helps a person’s clinicians manage their health throughout their life.

Making this vision a reality will require several changes to the way medicine is practiced and paid for today.

First, health systems, laboratories, and policymakers need to agree on how genomic data will be stored securely for decades and who can see it. Patients already trust online patient portals with their lab results and medical records, and genomic data can be held to the same standards of security and transparency.

These questions are already being actively worked on. Leading newborn sequencing programs, such as New York’s GUARDIAN study and England’s Generation Study, ask parents for opt-in consent, keep data under strict access controls, and are studying how long it should be kept. Leftover newborn screening blood spots have also been stored for years in many states, often without parents knowing, which is why consent and transparency have become central to this work. Any program that stores genomes, at birth or later, must start with fully informed consent: patients and parents should know what is kept, where, for how long and who may use it, and be free to say no.

Second, additional genetic counseling resources would need to support patients along their genomic health journeys, helping balance clinical needs, desires for information, and the familial implications of genomic insights. That support matters even more as care becomes increasingly patient-driven, with more people ordering tests themselves, reading their own results, and coming back with new questions.

Finally, and perhaps most important, insurers need a way to pay for evaluating a genome that has already been sequenced. Today, insurance can cover reanalysis, but there is no clear path to pay for reevaluation, the step that makes “test once, evaluate often” work. Paying for it would save insurers money, too, since it could replace repeat sequencing over a patient’s lifetime. Without reimbursement for prevention-oriented sequencing, genetic counseling, and genomic evaluation, we can’t improve equity in genomic testing.

Something I’ve seen again and again in the rare disease setting is that parents of a child without a diagnosis are almost always eager to share their child’s genetic data. They know that a match with another family somewhere in the world may be what finally explains what’s happening, and many new gene discoveries start exactly that way.

If we protect genomic data well and show people what sharing makes possible, more of us may come to see it the way these parents do: not as a risk to minimize, but as a path to answers, prevention, and cures.

Kelly Hagman, M.S., is a genetic counselor and vice president of medical affairs and strategic integration at Ambry Genetics, a Tempus company. She led the launch of the industry’s first clinical exome and has authored more than 55 peer-reviewed publications.

#5409. Weekly Rundown: Waystar integrates into Google Cloud’s Gemini for healthcare; Oracle debuts AI agents for clinical trials

Weekly Rundown: Waystar integrates into Google Cloud’s Gemini for healthcare; Oracle debuts AI agents for clinical trials" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Stay up to date on the latest in health tech, digital health and health AI news with this weekly brief. Read below for news from the week of Nov. 16 to 27.

Waystar said Tuesday it will integrate its AI-driven revenue cycle solutions into Google Cloud’s recently announced Gemini for healthcare solution.

The integration reflects an expanded partnership between Waystar and Google Cloud. Through it, users will have increased access to Waystar AltitudeAI innovations, advanced analytics and revenue cycle insights.

“By bringing Waystar's AI-powered revenue cycle capabilities into Gemini for healthcare, we're helping providers simplify some of the most complex operational and financial tasks in care delivery,” said Aashima Gupta, Google Cloud managing director of healthcare, in a statement. “Together, we are unifying data and workflows in a secure, governed workspace that drives better outcomes across the healthcare ecosystem.”

OpenAI is expanding ChatGPT’s health capabilities across various channels, it said Thursday.

The company’s Health feature is expanding to desktop app, Androids and its personal AI agents—dubbed dots.

ChatGPT Health is currently available to Free, Go, Plus, and Pro users in the U.S., while dots are available to Pro users.

Oracle launched a new agentic experience for life science organizations to improve clinical trial operations.

Oracle Life Science AI Agents is currently available for early adopters with a focus on portfolio monitoring, trial planning and conduct. The company plans to expand into clinical development domains, including data management, post-trial analytics and trial design.

Agents are designed to work with human oversight, executives say.

Oracle Health and Life Sciences EVP and General Manager Seema Verma said in a statement clinical development requires companies to “coordinate complex operational activity.”

“We are bringing AI-assisted intelligence into clinical trial operations to help organizations to monitor performance, identify emerging risks, and coordinate responses across the trial lifecycle,” Verma said. “By combining Oracle’s Life Sciences applications, AI-assisted capabilities, connected data services, on a secure, scalable cloud infrastructure, we are helping organizations coordinate clinical research workflows and operational decisions across their clinical trial environments.”

Agentic company Artera announced the roll out of an intake solution using AI Agents to collect, check and complete information throughout the patient visit.

Artera Intake has three core workflows, executives say: pre-visit intake, in-office and walk-in intake and complex form and consent digitization. The workflows are housed in a new Intake Hub, according to the Nov. 19 announcement.

Chief Product and Strategy Officer Zach Wood said in a statement what differentiates the solution from others is “where it starts.”

“Most intake solutions are built first, and providers have to change their workflows to fit them,” Wood said. “We start with the provider. We learn how their teams and patients actually move through intake, then build the agentic solution around that, together.”

Wood continued, “That starting point shapes everything that follows, and is designed to drive faster adoption, more completed intake and real value for practices.”

Amazon Connect Health announced Nov. 17 the launch of expanded patient access capabilities through the agentic solution.

As of the date of the announcement, four new capabilities are generally available to users: appointment management, prescription management, information assistance and password reset.

The company says the expansion builds on the foundation of Amazon Connect Health, which included patient verification, patient insights, ambient documentation and more.

One health system using the tool is Philadelphia-based Temple Health. AVP of Patient Access Joseph Alfonsi said in a statement the tool has handled patient verification on thousands of calls weekly since the system went live in June.

“Building on that success, we’re excited to expand agentic patient access capabilities for prescription management, portal password resets, and information assistance,” Alfonsi said. “Our patients shouldn’t have to wait until business hours—or wait on hold—to manage routine tasks. Now they can verify once and take care of everyday needs in a single call, any time of day, and our team can focus on the conversations where a human touch matters most.”

#5408. Opinion: Why medical students should keep going to class

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at the Stanford University School of Medicine.

This article is part of a new First Opinion series on the future of medical school.

By this time of year, the sky is black when I step outside. The day has carried me from lectures on gastrointestinal cancer disparities to TAing microbiology, from student government debates to helping free-clinic patients complete paperwork for expensive medications. With the cold nipping at my skin, I look back at the Stanford medical school building, its windows glowing. There is still so much to do, and even more to feel. I call my mother, my home base in human form. Three thousand miles away, she is preparing for bed. Circumstances beyond her control have kept her from taking a domestic flight for decades, let alone visit me in California. Her first question is always, “Did you remember to eat dinner?” Her second: “How were your classes today?”

I am a class-goer. Most of my classmates are, too, though preclinical lecture attendance among medical schools has been declining nationally since the pandemic and the Step 1 exam’s transition to pass/fail. Given the flexibility of recordings and the time students devote to service, research, and other commitments, I understand why some choose to study independently and firmly believe in preserving students’ freedom to make that choice.

For me, though, attending lectures in person has become an important part of feeling at home. It is the most powerful way I take care of my mental health and the classmates I have come to see as my newfound family. I would like to make the case why it could for other medical students, too.

Part of that happiness comes from my daily calls with my immigrant mother. What I learn gives me something to share with the woman who gave up her dream of becoming a clinician so I could pursue mine: dissecting a cadaver for the first time, suturing, administering flu vaccines for undocumented folks, wrapping wound dressing around an unhoused man’s arm. Putting these experiences into words is an exercise of understanding the unmistakably human profession I am entering.

I once worried that telling her the good parts of my day would make the distance between us more painful. Her unconditional love for me throughout the years has taught me otherwise. There are many students like me who left the comfort of our communities to pursue higher education. We should not have to compromise on maintaining relationships with loved ones, which influences medical student well-being and belonging.

In graduate school, where life is more independent, class also gives us a place to come together. During lecture breaks, I learn about friends advocating against the medical bloodletting of horseshoe crabs, making spaces more accessible to people with disabilities, and bringing care to under-resourced youth through mobile vans. We ask to become involved in one another’s work. Other days, happiness is resting my head on a friend’s shoulder, sharing my next bucket-list read — Bryant Lin’s “Sunshine: An Exploration of Living When You Are Dying” — or suggesting that we try the new cafe with robot baristas. It is remembering I am not walking this road alone.

Just as importantly, being physically present gives me opportunities to check in with others. As smartphones and artificial intelligence mediate more of our lives, I worry how easily we can grow used to being alone. Hard workers are remarkable at hiding stress. Intelligent people are good at forgetting to be kind to themselves. Class gives us a place, an excuse, not only to struggle through challenging coursework in real time together, but be part of one another’s lives. In between lectures, I am giving a friend a relationship pep talk as we complain about dating in the Bay Area. The next moment, I am making plans to cheer on another friend at a marathon. After lab, I am curled up on the reading room couch beside a peer whose mother has just been diagnosed with cancer. Our parents are getting older and sicker. It is infuriating. You would think learning medicine would brace us for inevitable losses. False. But knowing there is an abundance of people here to catch you is a peace in its own form.

In the classroom, I have also come to see my education as one I help shape. Conversations with professors following lectures have allowed me to successfully advocate to integrate various topics in our curriculum: sex differences in aortic stenosis pathophysiology, the relationship between ALDH2*2 deficiency and esophageal cancer, overdose response training. Medicine is evolving by the day, and these exchanges make education a collaboration between learners and teachers, showing students that our voices matter.

I think often of watching Celine Song’s “Past Lives” with my mother in December 2024, when I was still in New York. The film introduces in-yun, the idea that an encounter between two people is the result of countless threads from their past lives intertwining. Today, I still wonder if this, too, is a past life, and we are already something else to each other in the next. Perhaps in the next, I am the uninsured one who needs translation, and she is the medical student sitting across from me at the free clinic. In this life, it is 2 a.m. Eastern, and she is calling to ask about my day. It is 11 p.m. in California, and I am at the beach with friends, squinting into the Pacific because someone yelled that they spotted a whale. I imagine the animal’s song, sung at a frequency so low it travels for thousands of miles underwater, enough to carry me home.

I crave a big future, expansive in experience and generosity. For others, that may mean studying independently to make room for research, paid work, service, or rest. Those choices deserve grace.

For me, it begins with being physically present during these four brief years. Honoring my mother means doing good when her familiar applause is far away and nurturing the classmates who will become tomorrow’s doctors. Here is my chance to find where I fit, then widen that space for the next person. I don’t plan to squander a second of it.

Brian Zhang is a second-year M.D. student at Stanford University School of Medicine, where he currently serves as student body president.

The First Opinion series on the future of medical school will run through the end of 2026. Have an idea for a big or small way to change medical school? Email us.

#5407. Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute

Rural communities face heavier chronic disease burden, increasing pressure on PCPs: athenaInstitute" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Millennials living in rural areas have 42% more documented chronic conditions on average compared to those in other environments, a new report from athenaInstitute found.

And, millennials in rural communities are 47% more likely to have at least two chronic conditions. This heavier chronic disease burden extends to other generations as well, analysts note.

Half of Baby Boomers (50.4%) in rural areas have three or more documented conditions, which the report says is “on par” with non-rural individuals in the Silent and Greatest generations.

The 2026 Rural Ambulatory Care Report (PDF) analyzed athenahealth network data across 12.3 million rural patients between 2021 and 2025, as well as more than 30,000 clinicians and 1,861 rural practices across the entire U.S. Factors such as appointment activity, workforce composition, payments and more were examined.

Athenahealth CMO and athenaInstitute co-chair Nele Jessel, M.D., said in a statement the findings show while rural practices are not “standing still in the face of enormous challenges,” there are “limits to how much more they can absorb as patient needs continue to grow.”

“They are adapting how they deliver care and finding ways to keep patients connected to the care they need,” Jessel said. “With renewed focus on rural healthcare, there is a real opportunity to build on what is working by investing in the workforce, technology and models of care that can help these practices continue serving the communities that depend on them.”

Primary care physicians in rural areas have to wear multiple hats, as specialty care needs at practices are higher in rural communities.

The report found that primary care handles 68.7% of visits involving anxiety or depression diagnoses versus 55.1% in non-rural areas. Moreover, 25% of rural patients with documented anxiety or depression had a substance use disorder—up from 19.8% in non-rural communities.

Data shows rural and non-rural healthcare practices collected roughly the same share of what they were owed by insurers in 2025, but analysts note a difference in patient balances.

Rural practices collected about $70 of every $100 owed, while non-rural practices collected about $78—which analysts say is about a 10% gap.

Another potential source of financial vulnerability for rural practices is Medicaid. Medicaid covered 27.5% of rural visits, which analysts note leaves these practices more exposed to eligibility changes set to begin in 2027.

#5406. 10Web turns social media profiles into working commercial websites

Artificial intelligence website builder 10Web Inc. is introducing a new feature that it claims can automatically turn content from Instagram, TikTok, Etsy, Google Business Profiles and more than 30 other sources into functioning websites and online stores.

Called Start from Anything, the feature targets small businesses that lack the time and expertise to build their own websites. Users can paste a link to an existing online presence or upload files, and 10Web’s AI extracts the information needed to construct a website.

The system can convert photos and videos into galleries and product pages, use captions to populate product descriptions, and turn service information into dedicated pages. Business hours, addresses and location information can automatically populate contact pages, while social media posts can become news items and promotional offers.

10Web said its software also determines what functionality a website needs. Businesses offering services automatically receive booking capabilities, while those selling merchandise get online stores equipped to process orders and payments. Users can subsequently modify their websites by conversing with AI.

“Nobody opens a bakery because they love choosing plugins,” Chief Executive Narek Torosyan said in a statement. “Every question we ask an owner about software is a question we failed to answer ourselves.”

The service departs from the prompt-based approach that has dominated generative AI website development. Although prompts can create attractive websites, they require users to describe their businesses and often produce generic content that must subsequently be replaced or customized.

10Web’s approach is to reuse information businesses have already accumulated, such as photos, customer-facing descriptions, product catalogs and promotional materials.

The company said it tested the technology using publicly available content, converting a concept store‘s Instagram presence and a vintage retailer‘s TikTok account into online stores. It also generated websites from a vacation property‘s Google profile and a small business’s Facebook page.

The new capability builds on 10Web’s existing generative AI platform, which creates and manages websites using the open-source WordPress content management system.

In May 2025, the company introduced an application programming interface that allows developers and software providers to incorporate AI website generation into their applications. The platform uses specialized AI agents to handle different aspects of website development, including design, content creation and functionality.

10Web said the new feature includes hosting and is free to use for building and launching websites. The announcement did not specify charges for longer-term operation.

The company said it serves tens of thousands of customers worldwide and attracts between 50,000 and 60,000 new signups monthly.
